name: Adrienne E. Adams
comment_text: I am concerned about increases in parking demand within neighborhoods that are underserved by public transportation. The EA notes that although the CBD Tolling Program would result in “small changes in parking demand at transit facilities outside the CBD, corresponding to increased commuter rail and subway ridership,” no mitigation is needed. Chapter 4D, which discusses parking, only looks at neighborhoods where there is easy subway access, such as Flushing, Jamaica and Long Island City. It notes that the offstreet parking facilities in these neighborhoods are already heavily used and their streets are subject to existing regulations that limit long-term parking (alternate side parking regulations) and their being a reliable source of parking. However, the study does not specifically look at the commuter Long Island Railroad stations in eastern Queens – such as in Bellerose, St. Albans, and Douglaston. These stations are not easily accessible by transit and commuters residing in or within proximity to these neighborhoods, including from outside of New York City, who currently drive into Manhattan, are likely instead to drive to these LIRR stations to park-and-ride. I urge the agencies involved in the study to examine the potential impacts on these neighborhoods to determine whether any mitigation is needed to avoid any quality of life issues for persons that live near these stations related to increased traffic. The study also notes that any increase in parking or traffic in areas just north of 60th street in Manhattan will not adversely impact the quality of life for New Yorkers that live in that area. While the authorizing legislation requires a study for 18 months after the program takes effect in the surrounding areas, the implementing agencies should take proactive measures to improve traffic in the areas just north of the CBD before the program takes effect. THE COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF NEW YORK ADRIENNE E. ADAMS SPEAKER CITY HALL NEW YORK, NY 10007 TELEPHONE (212) 788-7210 September 8, 2022 FHWA - NY Division RE: CBDTP Leo W. O'Brien Federal Building 11A Clinton Ave., Suite 719 Albany, NY 12207 Dear Environmental Justice Stakeholders Working Group:

name: Adrienne E. Adams
comment_text: I am writing to express my concerns regarding the Central Business District (CBD) Tolling Program Environmental Assessment (EA) released on August 10, 2022 by the New York State Department of Transportation, the New York City Department of Transportation and the Federal Highway Administration. The EA does not sufficiently account for impacts on environmental justice communities and communities in the outer boroughs who cannot rely on mass transit to reach the CBD. The reality is that too many neighborhoods in New York City, like those in Southeast Queens that I represent, have long been underserved by the public transit system. It leaves them with limited transportation options beyond a reliance on automobiles. This persistent transit inequity is a major concern I share with many of my Council and elected colleagues representing communities in the outer boroughs. Many of these neighborhoods are also those that have historically been subjected to environmental racism. We must confront these realities in any planning process to enact a new tolling scheme.

name: Adrienne E. Adams
comment_text: While State law allows residents inside the CBD with an adjusted gross income of less than $60,000 to be eligible for a tax credit in the amount of the tolls paid during the taxable year, there are no measures to accommodate other low-income drivers, particularly those that may not have ready access to the E-Z Pass who typically are not eligible for any discounts under the present cashless tolling program. The Executive Summary of the EA notes that “the adverse effect on low-income drivers associated with the cost of the new toll would constitute a disproportionately high and adverse effect,” yet the study does not mention any efforts to lessen the burden of the CBD Tolling Program costs for these drivers. The EA should consider the potential economic impact of the CBD Tolling Program on lowincome drivers, and propose proactive solutions to reduce the burden.

name: Adrienne E. Adams
comment_text: The CBD Tolling Program is also likely to significantly impact the taxi and for-hire vehicle industry. At a time when drivers are already struggling to make ends meet and recover to pre-COVID-19 levels of business, the economic impact of a CBD Tolling Program could potentially be catastrophic to the industry. While the EA proposes some mitigation measures, such as working to connect drivers with licensing, training and job placement with the MTA or its vendors, and to allow the drivers to use vehicles to provide paratransit trips, the responsible agencies must take steps to prevent potential job displacement in the first place. The EA also found that the CBD Tolling Program would result in increased commercial truck traffic in both the Bronx and Staten Island, but determined that no air quality mitigation is needed. The EA estimates that air pollutants will increase in the Bronx and Staten Island as a result of the program, but only provides that agencies will monitor particulate matter to determine whether changes in air pollution can be attributed to the changes in traffic occurring after implementation of the CBD Tolling Program. Increases in truck traffic are of particular concern in communities near the Cross Bronx Expressway and RFK Bridge that already see high volumes of truck traffic and lack access to green space. The agencies involved in the project should undertake proactive mitigation measures to improve air quality in these areas. Residents in these areas already suffer from disproportionately higher rates of asthma and other respiratory issues, and a further increase in truck traffic will only exacerbate the problem. Any eventual CBD Tolling Program should not increase environmental harm for communities that have already been forced to disproportionately endure them.

name: Adrienne E. Adams
comment_text: There are a number of outstanding environmental and economic concerns that need to be addressed. While the program has some admirable goals to positively impact a number of residents throughout the city, it is critical that the agencies involved do not ignore the potential adverse impacts on low-income outer borough residents, especially those in environmental justice communities. Thank you for the opportunity to provide comment on the Environmental Assessment for the CBD Tolling Program. Sincerely, ADRIENNE E. ADAMS Speaker

name: Steve Alpert
comment_text: I live in Rockland County, NY and serve as a Village Trustee in Suffern, NY. The MTA has continuously been digging deeper and deeper into area residents’ pockets - A majority of whom do not even utilize the very services that the MTA is tasked with providing! Besides the highest cost commuter toll bridges in the country (currently between $13.10 and $20.34 round trip per car for MTA crossings like the Whitestone Bridge, Midtown Tunnel, and Battery Tunnel), among other things, the MTA also collects a $50 surcharge with every downstate NY State car registration renewal; they also collect a percentage of “Mortgage Recording Tax” on area home sales ($1,500 on a $500,000 mortgage), they also collect a 3/8% surcharge on top of all sales tax on all our purchases, and they even get an “income tax surcharge” within the 12-County MCTD area, called the “Metropolitan Commuter Transportation Mobility Tax” (MCTMT). Every few years, the MTA comes back to the State Government begging for another revenue stream….and the reason is simple: HUGE CRUSHING DEBT. The MTA has borrowed more money than dozens of entire countries - combined - - over $60 BILLION DOLLARS! The debt service on the outstanding amount - currently about $48 BILLION, is $3.2 Billion dollars per year according to what is posted on MTA’s website. This amount has doubled in just the last decade, leading the MTA to keep searching for the ever more revenue streams from the general public. Think about that: Before the MTA even uses a dime to provide the service they are actually responsible for, they first have to pay out billions of dollars in interest and principal each year! (Contrast this with prior to 1971, before they took on crushing debt, when the small 25 cent bridge tolls provided a *surplus* used to build additional bridges). Unfortunately, our State Government continues to allow the MTA to increase its borrowing, which has led to the current fiasco.

name: Steve Alpert
comment_text: Now, the MTA wants to institute so-called “Congestion Pricing”, charging drivers an additional $23 for the privilege of entering Manhattan south of 60th Street. They “claim” that this will reduce traffic in New York City.

name: Steve Alpert
comment_text: But think about it: the majority of drivers in New York already pay heavy tolls (as much as $20.34 round trip), not to mention the cost of parking in New York, typically about $50-$60 these days, if you include the current astronomical 18.375% parking tax. Clearly, cost is not a deterrent for many drivers who are well-heeled, and choose to drive every day in New York City. But in fairness, it might deter the occasional “middle class” visitor who was thinking about an occasional night out to visit a club, see a band, or have dinner with friends. This proposal will likely harm businesses that cater to middle class customers, but yet it will have virtually no effect on the majority of daytime traffic in Manhattan.

name: Steve Alpert
comment_text: Make no mistake. “Congestion Pricing”, which would even be in effect all weekend, is just another thinly veiled attempt to take more of residents’ money, to fund reckless debt floated by the MTA. A debt that has doubled in just the last 12 years, with virtually no improvement in service to show for it. If the MTA is granted the additional revenue stream for so-called “congestion pricing”, rest assured that this Public Authority will also waste this new revenue stream, just as they have squandered every other revenue stream they currently receive; of course having obtained each of the other revenue streams they currently get, by declaring that it is “absolutely needed”. The MTA operates without any real public scrutiny, and they have been granted one revenue stream after another, each time squandering the additional funding by further increasing their debt. This repeating cycle must stop! Say NO to congestion pricing!

name: Joann Ariola
comment_text: We are writing to ask that you withdraw your support for the Metropolitan Transportation Authority’s (MTA) “Central Business District Tolling Program.”

name: Joann Ariola
comment_text: The Environmental Assessment (EA) released by the MTA on August 10th makes it clear that the only objectives of the Central Business District Tolling Program (CBD) are to 1) reduce the miles vehicles travel within Central Manhattan by five percent; 2) reduce the number of cars coming into Central Manhattan by 10 percent; and 3) create a significant new funding source for the MTA. To create this marginal traffic benefit to Manhattan residents living within the proposed central business district, the CBD tolling program would charge an exorbitant toll for driving, which would effectively redisperse traffic congestion across other parts of New York City and the tri-state area, rather than reducing overall traffic. This toll, along with the negative environmental and financial impacts of this increased traffic in their communities, would disproportionately harm low and middle-income outer borough residents. Furthermore, at no point does the EA provide any conclusive evidence that this program would provide a source of revenue that is a stable and sustainable, nor does the MTA commit to specifically improving public transportation in areas of the city where it is significantly lacking.

name: Joann Ariola
comment_text: Once again, we should look to London, where the clogged main and arterial roadways across the city have had a particularly deleterious impact on communities outside the congestion pricing zone. Spillover traffic and motorists trying to avoid congestion now take circuitous routes through residential areas across the city and in neighborhoods in Outer London – what locals pejoratively call “rat running.” Rat running has led to traffic in otherwise quiet, arterial roads to double in the decade between 2009 and 2019, according to DfT data. The problem has gotten so bad that many borough officials began taking matters into their own hands, embarking on a new car-reduction plan called Low Traffic Neighborhoods by erecting barriers to prevent outside motorists from using their streets. The EA supports this:

name: Joann Ariola
comment_text: • Those travelling outside the CBD will see no reduction, and likely higher traffic volumes, despite the overwhelming number of New Yorkers who face congestion in Brooklyn, Queens, Staten Island, the Bronx, Nassau, on Long Island, the Hudson Valley, New Jersey, and Connecticut. In fact, even the optimistic data within the EA, shows traffic overall getting worse for Long Island, New Jersey, and Connecticut. In sum, the people who will pay the price get worse traffic. (Table ES-4) Mid-day and PM traffic volumes approaching the westbound George Washington Bridge will result in additional traffic throughout its northern Manhattan and South Bronx approaches. (4B-21) The EA estimates this will double pedestrian volume at already overcrowded NYC Subway stations in and around the central business district. (Table ES-4) The CBD Tolling Program Could Have Disastrous Health Impacts

name: Joann Ariola
comment_text: Even so, these estimates are troubling, especially when you look at the effect London’s congestion pricing has had on air pollution in Outer London and its suburbs over the last two decades. The toxic air pollution being caused by the increased traffic there is leading to nearly 4,000 premature deaths a year and children being born at lower birthweight, stunted lungs, and higher incidences of asthma, according to a recent study by the Imperial College of London. The CBD Tolling Program is a Regressive Tax

name: Joann Ariola
comment_text: Other concerning EA findings: • In every scenario, Staten Island will see more congestion from personal vehicles and trucks on highways and local streets. (Table 4A-25 & 4A-26) • In every alternative, the Bronx will see more traffic from thousands of additional commercial trucks, and in almost every scenario, the Bronx will see more traffic from personal vehicles. (Table 4A-28 &4A-29) Most of this additional traffic will be on the Cross Bronx Expressway, which has the distinction of having some of the worst asthma health outcomes in the nation. This tolling program will have little impact on the day-to-day life of wealthy commuters or residents within the Manhattan CBD. But the vast majority of the 1,856,000 people who enter the CBD by car each day – working- and middle-class residents of the outer boroughs and suburbs - and will now be forced to pay for these fortunate few. That is far greater than the entire population and beneficiaries living within the CBD. (EA Page 1-13). Even the EA begrudgingly admits, this toll would disproportionately impact on low-income New Yorkers, making this program a new regressive tax. (Table ES-4). Other EA findings:

name: Joann Ariola
comment_text: • The amount of total vehicle miles traveled throughout the 28-county study area will be reduced by between 0.2% and 0.4% by implementing any of the tolling scenarios as compared to taking no action, and by 2045, that number will only climb to a maximum of 0.5% at best. Meaning, it is a $1 billion annual tax on the region, without any regional benefit. (Table 4A-6, 4A-7 & 4A-14) The increase in daily commuting costs for auto drivers from New York City outside of the CBD will range from 7.9% to 37.2%, most significantly impacting lower income and minority drivers. Increases to Long Island, Hudson Valley, New Jersey, and Connecticut drivers will range from 5.8% to 26.5% (Table 4A-18) Drivers from New York City outside of the CBD can possibly face total daily tolls of up to $38.20, with the tolls having a disproportionate effect on lowincome families (Table 4A-19) No alternatives to generate $1 billion in revenue other than car-related fees were considered by the MTA that could spread the cost out more equitable and progressively through the regional population. The EA estimates the CBD Tolling Program would increase dangerous atmospheric pollutants – particulate matter, nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide, and volatile organic compounds – for Staten Island and the Bronx (Table 10-8). Considering the predicted increases in spillover traffic, particularly the hundreds of new trucks expected to fill the roads in these boroughs each hour, these estimates are laughably low and defy common sense (Table ES-4). Congestion Pricing Is Not a Budget Unicorn

name: Joann Ariola
comment_text: Congestion charge payments in London accounted for £232m (about $275 million) in revenue in 2021, or less than four percent of the total revenue for Transport for London (TfL), the city’s public transportation agency. Those figures came in after Mayor Sadiq Kahn increased the daily rate from £11.50 to £15 ($13 to $17.75) and adjusted the operating hours to includes 6PM-10PM and weekends to try to boost the agency’s income. The city’s congestion charge has failed to generate enough revenue to help TfL survive a precipitous drop in ridership and an economic downturn. The agency recently needed a $6 billion bailout from the federal government just to stay afloat. Considering London’s significantly higher traffic volumes, there is no chance the CBD Tolling Program would come close to generating the $1 billion MTA is projecting in the EA – especially when that figure does not incorporate exemptions that are being considered for New Jersey drivers, for-hire vehicles, and others. Given the MTA’s long, notorious history of fiscal mismanagement, cost-overruns, and failures to meet even the most generous project deadlines, it is simply magical

name: Joann Ariola
comment_text: Given all of these factors, to say that the Central Business District Tolling Program is problematic is an understatement: It is a disaster waiting to happen. We cannot in good conscience support a project that would be so harmful to so many New York City residents, and as leader of this state, we urge you to reconsider. Thank you for your time, courtesy, and consideration. Very truly yours, Joseph C. name: Diana Ayala
comment_text: The Central Business District Tolling Program (CBDTP), better known as congestion pricing, will benefit the greater New York City metropolitan area. While the overall impact of the CBDTP will be positive and will ultimately cause an overall reduction of mobile air toxins across the region, the proposed program increases air pollution within the Bronx. Even as the Bronx has taken steps forward with reducing carbon emissions, this is a step back for the neighborhoods surrounding the Cross Bronx Expressway, due to the increased air pollution from vehicles on the highway. The MTA's report notes an overall decline in air pollution across the city and region, but an increase for the Bronx. This is primarily due to increased vehicle miles traveled on the Cross Bronx Expressway, and the reality is there would be an additional increase on other highways, including the Bruckner Expressway and Major Deegan, through secondary transportation pressure, even if the methodology doesn’t show an increase. The CBDTP is therefore an issue affecting health, equity, and environmental justice issues for the communities we represent, which have historically taken on more than their fair share for decades. In order to have our support for the CBDTP, these Bronx neighborhoods need to see direct benefits that will result in a reduction of mobile air toxins. The best solution would be prioritizing the capital funding for the capping of the Cross Bronx Expressway. Money was allocated as part of the bipartisan infrastructure bill that Senator Chuck Schumer and Congressman Ritchie Torres were both instrumental in getting passed, but the project will need additional resources and it should be prioritized by the city and state. It is also important that the deck on top of the Cross Bronx provide additional long-term benefits, such as providing green space or by creating a public transportation light rail line. This line could provide an east-west railway link stretching from Washington Heights to Parkchester, creating connections across eight subway lines and serving the nearly 600,000 people that live in adjacent neighborhoods. In addition to fully funding the Cross Bronx decking, further priority should be given to projects that would reduce greenhouse gas emissions, such as providing free buses across the entire city, or, at a minimum, within Bronx environmental justice areas harmed by the CBDTP to further incentivize public transportation options for residents that need it the most. The city should also pass electric vehicle supportive legislation that will remove hurdles for where electric vehicle charging stations can be located and provide opportunities for electric vehicle investment across the city. This will encourage the transition to electric vehicles, which will be key to reducing emissions within the city. Other ways the city can support these environmental justice areas include prioritizing and further incentivizing renewable energy bonuses for building upgrades. The Bronx has many buildings with low-income residents and the city needs to support improvements to these buildings in order for building upgrades to happen. For NYCHA buildings, the city needs to prioritize and fully fund renewable energy upgrades. OFFICE OF THE BRONX BOROUGH PRESIDENT - 851 GRAND CONCOURSE, SUITE 301, BRONX, NY 10451 - (718) 590-3500

name: Diana Ayala
comment_text: We acknowledge that the CBDTP will be a benefit for much of the city, but the Bronx has been burdened by the Cross Bronx since its construction under the notion that it is good for the region as a whole. With the CBDTP adding to that historical burden, it is time the Bronx receives major capital improvements that will provide real health benefits in these environmental justice communities. name: District Leader Lee Berman
comment_text: Hi. I'm Lee Berman, District Leader from the Lower East Side of Manhattan, a Transit desert. And I represent thousands of residents within the Central Business District, many of whom have lived here for generations that would be irreparably and negatively affected by this ridiculous plan. If this illconceived and discriminatory plan is approved, an exemption for all residents who live in Lower Manhattan must be granted. Those of us who live here, who, unlike as stated in your Environmental Assessment, do not have the ability to just pick up and move to outside the zone, should not have to pay an additional tax on topof the taxes and fees we are already forced to pay to live here. The purported credit for those earning under $60,000 will still require them to fork over this tax and then wait to get a refund when they file their income taxes. And if you earn one dollar over the 60,000-dollar threshold, you're totally screwed. Many in this very community, this Transit desert, require the use of a car; whether to get to and from their job, to get to doctors' appointments, to pick up their children from after-school programs or extracurricular activities, or who wish to visit family who live too far to visit on unsafe and unreliable mass transit. Or because taking a family of four, or six, or eight, on buses and trains for two to three-plus hours each way is not possible for them. You're going to tax Orthodox Jews who drive to Brooklyn to buy kosher food. In Chinatown, residents can drive to Sunset Park, get to other Chinatown to shop for their families because they don't want to risk being victims of hate crimes on the subway. Congestion pricing will further tax the working middle class, the lower income families of Lower Manhattan. One of the things the pandemic has shown is that more and more residents who can afford to, will leave. But too many of us in Lower Manhattan do not have that luxury, no matter what the anti-car fanatics claim. Every Lower Manhattan resident will now have to pay higher prices for everyday goods and services, including those who can least afford to. That includes those of us living in poverty and the disabled. Our local bodegas, supermarkets and other stores are not going to eat the increased fees they have to pay for deliveries. Every store is going to pass along the cost of their suppliers' transportation to all of us in Lower Manhattan. And while the bougie side -listen, those of you making this decision to act like communities can afford it, we cannot. You insult New Yorkers' intelligence by telling us that the MTA, which for generations have squandered our tax dollars and fares to the tune of hundreds of billions of dollars over the years, will actually spend this newfound tax to actually improve transit and not waste it. If you believe that, then I have a bridge to sell you. No. We will not let you bleed the workingclass people of Lower Manhattan dry so that you can continue the wasteful spending of the MTA on the backs of our residents. Money was allocated as part of the bipartisan infrastructure bill that Senator Chuck Schumer and Congressman Ritchie Torres were both instrumental in getting passed, but the project will need additional resources and it should be prioritized by the city and state. It is also important that the deck on top of the Cross Bronx provide additional long-term benefits, such as providing green space or by creating a public transportation light rail line. This line could provide an east-west railway link stretching from Washington Heights to Parkchester, creating connections across eight subway lines and serving the nearly 600,000 people that live in adjacent neighborhoods. In addition to fully funding the Cross Bronx decking, further priority should be given to projects that would reduce greenhouse gas emissions, such as providing free buses across the entire city, or, at a minimum, within Bronx environmental justice areas harmed by the CBDTP to further incentivize public transportation options for residents that need it the most. The city should also pass electric vehicle supportive legislation that will remove hurdles for where electric vehicle charging stations can be located and provide opportunities for electric vehicle investment across the city. This will encourage the transition to electric vehicles, which will be key to reducing emissions within the city. Other ways the city can support these environmental justice areas include prioritizing and further incentivizing renewable energy bonuses for building upgrades. The Bronx has many buildings with low-income residents and the city needs to support improvements to these buildings in order for building upgrades to happen. For NYCHA buildings, the city needs to prioritize and fully fund renewable energy upgrades. OFFICE OF THE BRONX BOROUGH PRESIDENT - 851 GRAND CONCOURSE, SUITE 301, BRONX, NY 10451 - (718) 590-3500

name: Frank Borelli
comment_text: As a recent example, last month, I won the Broadway Lottery to see a Friday evening performance of "Into the Woods". My daughter and I decided to take the train into Manhattan. She only got out of work at 3:45, so we couldn't take anything that left before 4:30pm. We first checked the schedule for the closest train station to our house: the Nanuet station on the Pascack Valley Line of NJ Transit. That idea was quickly scrapped when we discovered that there are no trains going into Penn Station from 3:55pm until 9:20pm. We then looked at the schedule for the Suffern train station on the Bergen/Main line of NJ Transit. Those trains at least gave us an option to get into the City. We had the option of a train that left at 4:55pm or 5:46pm that would get us into the City early enough to get to the theater in time. Unfortunately, that train station is significantly further away from my house, and we had to factor in well over 25 minutes to travel from my house to get to the Suffern train station. Due to a teenager taking the fastest shower ever and the most incredible luck with traffic lights, we managed to get to the Suffern train station with 5 minutes to spare. We were able to board the 4:55 train. We were not yet done with the stress from our ride. Rockland County does not have a one-ride way to get to Penn Station. The Bergen/Main line was only a local trip that arrived at Secaucus Junction at 5:54pm. When we arrived at Secaucus Junction, there was a mad dash by all of the passengers of our train to go to a different part of the station where we were able to switch to a train to take us from Secaucus to the City. We finally arrived at NY Penn Station at approximately 6:18pm. We then walked roughly 20 minutes to get to Times Square and the Theater District. We didn't have much time for more than a quick takeout bite to eat before heading to the theater and seeing the show (a fantastic performance, by the way)! Then it was time to get home. The show let out at roughly 11pm. We (along with what must have been a few hundred other people) made our way back to Penn Station. And there we waited. There was an 11:06pm train (which we weren't able to catch because we were still in the theater) followed by a 12:02am train. So we spent roughly 45 minutes waiting in Penn Station. From roughly 12:02am12:11am, we travelled to Secaucus. We then had 7 minutes to find the correct track for the Bergen/Main line, and at 12:18am, we were on our way to Rockland county. We were scheduled to arrive in Suffern at 1:19am (we actually arrived about 10 minutes late). We then had to walk to our car (my car was parked in a lot a few blocks away from the train station). And then the 25 minute drive home. We got home shortly before 2am. We had a fantastic time in the City, but: It took us roughly 2 hours to get from my house to the Theater District via mass transit plus 3 hours from when the show ended to get back home. My daughter and I spent 5 hours dealing with mass transit to see a show that runs 2 hours and 45 minutes. By contrast, my sister happened to win the Broadway Lottery this month for Hadestown (another fantastic show), but she drove this time. It took us approximately 45 minutes to drive each way, and around 15 minutes at the parking garage. So we spent a total of 2 hours round trip commuting by car. In summary -- My experience taking mass transit from Rockland County took me 5 hours to travel

name: Frank Borelli
comment_text: I applaud the state trying to encourage people to take mass transit. However, the state must first ensure that mass transit is a viable option before penalizing people for not using it. Asking someone to spend more than twice as long to take mass transit vs paying an expensive surcharge for "congestion pricing" is not being done in good faith. My friends in Westchester can be in NYC in less than an hour. Those of us in Rockland should have similar options. When the TZ Bridge was being rebuilt, I was thrilled at the plans for a train to connect Rockland with Metro North. That didn't happen. I was thrilled when NY and NJ were talking about a tunnel to allow one-stop trains on NJ Transit. That didn't happen. Congestion pricing shouldn't take effect until there is a viable mass transit for the entire metro area. If that is not possible, then there should be an exception made for Rockland County residents who simply do not have a realistic option to take mass transit into the City. Otherwise, this is not a means to encourage more people to use mass transit, but rather an unfair tax on those of us who live in Rockland county.

comment_text: ST September 9, 2022 Honorable Kathy Hochul Governor State of New York 633 3rd Ave 38th floor New York, NY 10017 Dear Governor Hochul:

name: Joseph C. Borelli
comment_text: We are writing to ask that you withdraw your support for the Metropolitan Transportation Authority’s (MTA) “Central Business District Tolling Program.”

name: Joseph C. Borelli
comment_text: The Environmental Assessment (EA) released by the MTA on August 10th makes it clear that the only objectives of the Central Business District Tolling Program (CBD) are to 1) reduce the miles vehicles travel within Central Manhattan by five percent; 2) reduce the number of cars coming into Central Manhattan by 10 percent; and 3) create a significant new funding source for the MTA. To create this marginal traffic benefit to Manhattan residents living within the proposed central business district, the CBD tolling program would charge an exorbitant toll for driving, which would effectively redisperse traffic congestion across other parts of New York City and the tri-state area, rather than reducing overall traffic. This toll, along with the negative environmental and financial impacts of this increased traffic in their communities, would disproportionately harm low and middle-income outer borough residents. Furthermore, at no point does the EA provide any conclusive evidence that this program would provide a source of revenue that is a stable and sustainable, nor does the MTA commit to specifically improving public transportation in areas of the city where it is significantly lacking.

name: Joseph C. Borelli
comment_text: Once again, we should look to London, where the clogged main and arterial roadways across the city have had a particularly deleterious impact on communities outside the congestion pricing zone. Spillover traffic and motorists trying to avoid congestion now take circuitous routes through residential areas across the city and in neighborhoods in Outer London – what locals pejoratively call “rat running.” Rat running has led to traffic in otherwise quiet, arterial roads to double in the decade between 2009 and 2019, according to DfT data. The problem has gotten so bad that many borough officials began taking matters into their own hands, embarking on a new car-reduction plan called Low Traffic Neighborhoods by erecting barriers to prevent outside motorists from using their streets. The EA supports this:

name: Joseph C. Borelli
comment_text: • Those travelling outside the CBD will see no reduction, and likely higher traffic volumes, despite the overwhelming number of New Yorkers who face congestion in Brooklyn, Queens, Staten Island, the Bronx, Nassau, on Long Island, the Hudson Valley, New Jersey, and Connecticut. In fact, even the optimistic data within the EA, shows traffic overall getting worse for Long Island, New Jersey, and Connecticut. In sum, the people who will pay the price get worse traffic. (Table ES-4) Mid-day and PM traffic volumes approaching the westbound George Washington Bridge will result in additional traffic throughout its northern Manhattan and South Bronx approaches. (4B-21) The EA estimates this will double pedestrian volume at already overcrowded NYC Subway stations in and around the central business district. (Table ES-4) The CBD Tolling Program Could Have Disastrous Health Impacts

name: Joseph C. Borelli
comment_text: Even so, these estimates are troubling, especially when you look at the effect London’s congestion pricing has had on air pollution in Outer London and its suburbs over the last two decades. The toxic air pollution being caused by the increased traffic there is leading to nearly 4,000 premature deaths a year and children being born at lower birthweight, stunted lungs, and higher incidences of asthma, according to a recent study by the Imperial College of London. The CBD Tolling Program is a Regressive Tax

name: Joseph C. Borelli
comment_text: Other concerning EA findings: • In every scenario, Staten Island will see more congestion from personal vehicles and trucks on highways and local streets. (Table 4A-25 & 4A-26) • In every alternative, the Bronx will see more traffic from thousands of additional commercial trucks, and in almost every scenario, the Bronx will see more traffic from personal vehicles. (Table 4A-28 &4A-29) Most of this additional traffic will be on the Cross Bronx Expressway, which has the distinction of having some of the worst asthma health outcomes in the nation. This tolling program will have little impact on the day-to-day life of wealthy commuters or residents within the Manhattan CBD. But the vast majority of the 1,856,000 people who enter the CBD by car each day – working- and middle-class residents of the outer boroughs and suburbs - and will now be forced to pay for these fortunate few. That is far greater than the entire population and beneficiaries living within the CBD. (EA Page 1-13). Even the EA begrudgingly admits, this toll would disproportionately impact on low-income New Yorkers, making this program a new regressive tax. (Table ES-4). Other EA findings:

name: Joseph C. Borelli
comment_text: • The amount of total vehicle miles traveled throughout the 28-county study area will be reduced by between 0.2% and 0.4% by implementing any of the tolling scenarios as compared to taking no action, and by 2045, that number will only climb to a maximum of 0.5% at best. Meaning, it is a $1 billion annual tax on the region, without any regional benefit. (Table 4A-6, 4A-7 & 4A-14) The increase in daily commuting costs for auto drivers from New York City outside of the CBD will range from 7.9% to 37.2%, most significantly impacting lower income and minority drivers. Increases to Long Island, Hudson Valley, New Jersey, and Connecticut drivers will range from 5.8% to 26.5% (Table 4A-18) Drivers from New York City outside of the CBD can possibly face total daily tolls of up to $38.20, with the tolls having a disproportionate effect on lowincome families (Table 4A-19) No alternatives to generate $1 billion in revenue other than car-related fees were considered by the MTA that could spread the cost out more equitable and progressively through the regional population. The EA estimates the CBD Tolling Program would increase dangerous atmospheric pollutants – particulate matter, nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide, and volatile organic compounds – for Staten Island and the Bronx (Table 10-8). Considering the predicted increases in spillover traffic, particularly the hundreds of new trucks expected to fill the roads in these boroughs each hour, these estimates are laughably low and defy common sense (Table ES-4). Congestion Pricing Is Not a Budget Unicorn

name: Joseph C. Borelli
comment_text: Congestion charge payments in London accounted for £232m (about $275 million) in revenue in 2021, or less than four percent of the total revenue for Transport for London (TfL), the city’s public transportation agency. Those figures came in after Mayor Sadiq Kahn increased the daily rate from £11.50 to £15 ($13 to $17.75) and adjusted the operating hours to includes 6PM-10PM and weekends to try to boost the agency’s income. The city’s congestion charge has failed to generate enough revenue to help TfL survive a precipitous drop in ridership and an economic downturn. The agency recently needed a $6 billion bailout from the federal government just to stay afloat. Considering London’s significantly higher traffic volumes, there is no chance the CBD Tolling Program would come close to generating the $1 billion MTA is projecting in the EA – especially when that figure does not incorporate exemptions that are being considered for New Jersey drivers, for-hire vehicles, and others. Given the MTA’s long, notorious history of fiscal mismanagement, cost-overruns, and failures to meet even the most generous project deadlines, it is simply magical

name: Joseph C. Borelli
comment_text: Given all of these factors, to say that the Central Business District Tolling Program is problematic is an understatement: It is a disaster waiting to happen. We cannot in good conscience support a project that would be so harmful to so many New York City residents, and as leader of this state, we urge you to reconsider. Thank you for your time, courtesy, and consideration. Very truly yours, Joseph C. comment_text: Testimony of New York City Council Member Erik Bottcher to the Traffic Mobility Review Board Regarding Proposed Central Business District Tolling Program September 6, 2022

name: Erik Bottcher
comment_text: Thank you for the opportunity to submit testimony in support of the proposed Central Business District Tolling Program, which, if approved, would help our city address the growing problems of traffic congestion, noise and air pollution, and an underfunded public transit system. As the Council Member representing District 3, which is located almost entirely within the Central Business District, I have been a longtime supporter of congestion pricing as a means of raising desperately needed funds to maintain and expand our public transportation infrastructure as well as reducing the volume of unnecessary car and truck traffic in our community. Finally, as the Council Member representing much of the West Side of Manhattan, I oppose exemptions for New Jersey residents. A large percentage of the traffic congestion in Council District 3 consists of cars with New Jersey license plates. This is in spite of the numerous options for public transportation, including the PATH train, New Jersey Transit, and the Port Authority Bus Terminal. Exempting New Jersey residents from the program would only exacerbate congestion and issues of air and noise quality in our district. Thank you again for the opportunity to submit this testimony in favor of this desperately needed program. I know the Board has many difficult decisions ahead of you and I appreciate your consideration. Erik Bottcher Council Member, District 3 Every neighborhood in Council District 3 is frequently clogged with car and truck traffic. Ninth Avenue in Hell’s Kitchen, Sixth Avenue in Chelsea and Varick Street in the South Village/Hudson Square are examples of streets that are frequently besieged by bumper to bumper traffic, especially at rush hour. More traffic enforcement agents, changes to street markings or ‘no honking’ signs will not solve the problem. The only long-term solution is to reduce the volume of vehicular traffic in our district.

name: Erik Bottcher
comment_text: There are a few specific groups that I hope the Board will consider as they work to create and implement this program. Consideration should be made for residents who live within the Central Business District. Many residents who live within the area, for personal or professional reasons, need to drive to and from their home and should not be penalized for living in an area that serves as a destination for others. Another group that should receive special consideration are yellow taxi drivers. Yellow cabs are iconic to New York City, and they have suffered extraordinary financial hardship in recent years. I am concerned that an additional surcharge will be ruinous for the yellow cab industry. Additionally, I hope the board will take into consideration measures that would incentivize the use of electric vehicles, until the technology is more widely adopted. As we face a worsening climate crisis, we need to use all tools at our disposal to reduce the use of fossil fuels.

name: Gale Brewer
comment_text: Thank you very much. I am Gale Brewer. I represent the Upper West Side in the 6th District, and I'm just going to summarize some of the points. I want to say also in anticipation, just the other day, we had a meeting on the Upper West Side that I convened. Secondly, on the disability front, we know that if one has a current license plate indicating disability, you will be exempt. But there are others, as you heard earlier, going to the hospitals. comment_text: COMMITTEES THE COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF NEW YORK GALE A. BREWER COUNCIL MEMBER, 6TH DISTRICT, MANHATTAN CONSUMER AND WORKER PROTECTION FINANCE

name: Councilmember Gale Brewer
comment_text: My name is Gale A. Brewer and I represent the Upper West Side in the 6th Council District. West 60th Street is in my district.

name: Councilmember Gale Brewer
comment_text: I support the concept of congestion pricing; I voted for it as a Council Member in 2008; and I supported it as the Manhattan Borough President in 2019 when I held a hearing on residential parking in anticipation of congestion pricing going into effect. I have enclosed a copy of my office’s report on the topic of residential parking in seven cities worldwide. Addressing congestion, emissions, and funding needs for the public transportation system are critical to New York City’s long-term wellbeing. To meet the outlined goals, a durable and comprehensive congestion pricing program must be created.

name: Councilmember Gale Brewer
comment_text: I have read some of the 1000-page environmental assessment, initiated a discussion on zoom with the local elected officials, staff of Community Board 7, representatives of the Business Improvement Districts, local hospital and college staff, and other stakeholders to collaborate and coordinate on mutual concerns; and fielded hundreds of calls, e-mails and letters from constituents and institutions concerned about the impact of congestion pricing on them. Months ago, as Manhattan Borough President, I advocated that a member of the community who is Manhattan resident and a transportation expert be appointed to the Traffic Mobility Review Board, and I was disappointed that such a person was not appointed. Communication To show good faith to the customers of the subways and the buses, the MTA must run a faster, cleaner, and safer system before implementing congestion pricing to demonstrate what the billions will buy. I have called for 6-minute arrival times for all subways lines, which would attract riders through convenience and improved public safety. Andrew Albert, who represents riders on the MTA Board, points out that a $52 billion MTA capital plan will bring new cars, ADA accessibility, improved signals, better platforms, cleaning devices etc. and the MTA will The MTA must be transparent with any funds and show that the money is in a lockbox for transit. How will this effort be demonstrated? What metrics will be used? What is the required reporting for congestion pricing? Citizen Budget Commission recommends that the MTA monitor and report congestion pricing outcomes and operational metrics to inform future policy adjustments. Traffic in the West 60th Street Area – and Above The Department of Transportation must look very carefully at the traffic patterns in the West 60s street area before any decisions are made. Currently, a driver going down Broadway cannot turn left until 61st Street because West 64th Street is closed to any such turn. Residents were furious when this was initiated and continue to be frustrated. How is this being studied? What is the impact? How is Lincoln Center and its peak times incorporated into the planning?

name: Councilmember Gale Brewer
comment_text: The Lincoln Square BID has studied the garage spaces in the area of the West 60s. There are only about 3700 spaces. As of August 2022, there are 16 garages – 15 of which are located north of 60th Street - with 3,779 spots. In summary, all 16 of the parking garages offer monthly parking, at an average cost of $684/month, and two are booked with monthly parkers. 15 offer daily rates that vary. 11 offer 24-hour parking. In the summer months, the garages seemed half full, but many people were away. Note that there are other garages outside of the BID area. This BID has communicated to me that they are opposed to congestion pricing in its current format.

name: Councilmember Gale Brewer
comment_text: The Columbus Avenue BID which is located above the 60th Street cut off stated that local businesses had not voiced concern except for their fear that even more trucks would double park and instead of just quickly unloading their delivery, they would unload bicycles and packages so as to bike below 60th Street, leaving the truck in the same spot for a long period of time.

name: Councilmember Gale Brewer
comment_text: Residents are observing many out of state license plates on cars that park regularly on the streets of the Upper West Side; residents should register their car in NYC and not at the address of a summer home. How can this be enforced?

name: Councilmember Gale Brewer
comment_text: There are concerns about what is going to happen north of 60th Street. Residents of West Harlem and Harlem neighborhoods already see people parking and taking public transportation or cabs to go south, and they think it will only get worse. They think people are going to drive in, park their car, and hop on the subway, bus, bike, or scooter. Knowing that there is already a parking shortage and believing it will get worse, some people are advocating for a residential parking permit system.

name: Councilmember Gale Brewer
comment_text: Placard abuse must be stopped concurrently with implementation of congestion parking. Residents point out that during the worst of the pandemic, few cars were on the roads, and many of them traveled well above the speed limit. They worry that the same will occur with congestion pricing. I do not think that the streets will empty of vehicles, but speed restrictions must be enforced. Will all speed cameras be installed and working when congestion pricing is in effect? Although I support Central Business District Tolling Program (CBDTP), as the Traffic Mobility Review Board deliberates on how best to implement the CBDTP, I urge the members to take into consideration issues of importance that will lead to positive implementation.

name: Councilmember Gale Brewer
comment_text: Exemptions Requested Hospitals are understaffed, especially during the night shift. Many healthcare workers commute by car at late hours or leave during the night and drive because they live far away. These employees are dependent on their car for evening and night work, and either do not feel safe, or cannot rely on public transportation during these hours. Mt. Sinai West/Roosevelt Hospital is located at 1000 Tenth Ave which is at 59th Street, just inside the 60th Street “must pay” zone. The hospital is requesting an exemption for these workers.

name: Councilmember Gale Brewer
comment_text: Will hospitals have funding to reimburse appropriate parties for congestion tolls? Service delivery workers rely on transportation, and some of them are required to drive for their jobs. 1199 represents healthcare workers on Rikers Island. If the pharmacist doesn’t have the drugs they need, they must go into the city to see if the medication is available elsewhere. Fordham University at Lincoln Center which is on the north side of West 60th Street at 113 West 60th Street has some of the same concerns. Human service programs deliver meals up and down Manhattan as well as city-wide, and they want to be exempted. I recently delivered meals with Encore, traveling from West 49 Street to West 94 Street to deliver meals to homebound seniors. The Coalition for the Homeless (CFTH) delivers meals and has asked for an exemption for its delivery trucks. One of CFTH’s programs that will be directly affected by these additional costs is their Grand Central Food Program which runs vans in Manhattan and (1) in the Bronx to provide over 1,100 meals to hungry street homeless and working poor New Yorkers every night of the year. These vans will at times also provide clothing, such as coats and socks, book bags with school supplies and other items that they receive throughout the year. There are many distribution stops located within the Central Business District for all of the human service programs and vans enter and travel within the district multiple times each day and night. The resulting additional tolls would place a significant financial burden on the agencies. Many of these services are funded by City and State contracts, but there is no mechanism to cover this cost for the non-profits. Yellow taxis already pay a congestion charge ($2.50) for entering Manhattan below 96th Street. I urge a full exemption from any fee for these vehicles. People who live in the zone should get a credit regarding the congestion fee; and the $60,000 income limit for a tax rebate should be raised and the way in which they are reimbursed should be reviewed. It is often difficult to get a tax rebate. The MTA should review what one constituent suggested: implement an exemption, carve out or special resident toll that would continue to encourage Manhattan residents who live outside the congestion zone and want to leave Manhattan to take the most environmentally efficient route out of Manhattan to go to NJ and LI, even if travel into the CBD zone is necessary. These types of ‘resident’ programs already exist for the Rockaways and Staten Island and can be easily implemented using E-ZPass and cars registered to certain Manhattan zip codes. This type of resident plan should be incorporated into the final plan developed for implementation. Currently, people with disabilities who have disability license plates will not pay the toll. But many others have a disability that may be temporary, they need to get to a medical appointment and the MTA should explore how such individuals can be accommodated. Economic Impact Unless congestion pricing varies by hours/ times of day there be will impact on evening industries like theatres and restaurants. New York City depends on bridge and tunnel folks, tourists and visitors, and people from the tristate area. Tolls should be varied based on the day of the week and the time of the day, with the goal of reducing congestion. This must be consistent and clearly communicated to drivers. There should not be a dynamic pricing model implemented similar to surge pricing used by for hire vehicles. If there is a variance by time of day, MTA must identify the most effective way to balance peak and off-peak tolls to meet congestion/ congestion/ revenue goals while maximizing revenue.

name: Councilmember Gale Brewer

comment_text: By statute, the CBD Tolling Program must have variable tolling (see Section 1704-a “Central business district toll” in Appendix 2B of the EA). Our communities lack viable public transportation services to effectively, safely and reliably travel into Manhattan. name: Kenneth Burgos
comment_text: The Central Business District Tolling Program (CBDTP), better known as congestion pricing, will benefit the greater New York City metropolitan area. While the overall impact of the CBDTP will be positive and will ultimately cause an overall reduction of mobile air toxins across the region, the proposed program increases air pollution within the Bronx. Even as the Bronx has taken steps forward with reducing carbon emissions, this is a step back for the neighborhoods surrounding the Cross Bronx Expressway, due to the increased air pollution from vehicles on the highway. The MTA's report notes an overall decline in air pollution across the city and region, but an increase for the Bronx. This is primarily due to increased vehicle miles traveled on the Cross Bronx Expressway, and the reality is there would be an additional increase on other highways, including the Bruckner Expressway and Major Deegan, through secondary transportation pressure, even if the methodology doesn’t show an increase. The CBDTP is therefore an issue affecting health, equity, and environmental justice issues for the communities we represent, which have historically taken on more than their fair share for decades. In order to have our support for the CBDTP, these Bronx neighborhoods need to see direct benefits that will result in a reduction of mobile air toxins. The best solution would be prioritizing the capital funding for the capping of the Cross Bronx Expressway. Money was allocated as part of the bipartisan infrastructure bill that Senator Chuck Schumer and Congressman Ritchie Torres were both instrumental in getting passed, but the project will need additional resources and it should be prioritized by the city and state. It is also important that the deck on top of the Cross Bronx provide additional long-term benefits, such as providing green space or by creating a public transportation light rail line. This line could provide an east-west railway link stretching from Washington Heights to Parkchester, creating connections across eight subway lines and serving the nearly 600,000 people that live in adjacent neighborhoods. In addition to fully funding the Cross Bronx decking, further priority should be given to projects that would reduce greenhouse gas emissions, such as providing free buses across the entire city, or, at a minimum, within Bronx environmental justice areas harmed by the CBDTP to further incentivize public transportation options for residents that need it the most. The city should also pass electric vehicle supportive legislation that will remove hurdles for where electric vehicle charging stations can be located and provide opportunities for electric vehicle investment across the city. This will encourage the transition to electric vehicles, which will be key to reducing emissions within the city. Other ways the city can support these environmental justice areas include prioritizing and further incentivizing renewable energy bonuses for building upgrades. The Bronx has many buildings with low-income residents and the city needs to support improvements to these buildings in order for building upgrades to happen. For NYCHA buildings, the city needs to prioritize and fully fund renewable energy upgrades. OFFICE OF THE BRONX BOROUGH PRESIDENT - 851 GRAND CONCOURSE, SUITE 301, BRONX, NY 10451 - (718) 590-3500

name: David Carr
comment_text: We are writing to ask that you withdraw your support for the Metropolitan Transportation Authority’s (MTA) “Central Business District Tolling Program.”

name: David Carr
comment_text: The Environmental Assessment (EA) released by the MTA on August 10th makes it clear that the only objectives of the Central Business District Tolling Program (CBD) are to 1) reduce the miles vehicles travel within Central Manhattan by five percent; 2) reduce the number of cars coming into Central Manhattan by 10 percent; and 3) create a significant new funding source for the MTA. To create this marginal traffic benefit to Manhattan residents living within the proposed central business district, the CBD tolling program would charge an exorbitant toll for driving, which would effectively redisperse traffic congestion across other parts of New York City and the tri-state area, rather than reducing overall traffic. This toll, along with the negative environmental and financial impacts of this increased traffic in their communities, would disproportionately harm low and middle-income outer borough residents. Furthermore, at no point does the EA provide any conclusive evidence that this program would provide a source of revenue that is a stable and sustainable, nor does the MTA commit to specifically improving public transportation in areas of the city where it is significantly lacking.

name: David Carr
comment_text: Once again, we should look to London, where the clogged main and arterial roadways across the city have had a particularly deleterious impact on communities outside the congestion pricing zone. Spillover traffic and motorists trying to avoid congestion now take circuitous routes through residential areas across the city and in neighborhoods in Outer London – what locals pejoratively call “rat running.” Rat running has led to traffic in otherwise quiet, arterial roads to double in the decade between 2009 and 2019, according to DfT data. The problem has gotten so bad that many borough officials began taking matters into their own hands, embarking on a new car-reduction plan called Low Traffic Neighborhoods by erecting barriers to prevent outside motorists from using their streets. The EA supports this:

name: David Carr

CUSICK Assemblyman 63rd District Richmond County Veterans’ Affairs Ways and Means STATEMENT Central Business District Tolling Program I’d like to start by thanking the MTA for holding these public meetings to give elected officials and the public the opportunity to voice our concerns as you move forward with congestion pricing.

name: Michael Cusick
comment_text: Throughout the years I have spoken about my concerns with congestion pricing. While there are environmental benefits with respect to taking cars off the road, but as a Staten Islander and a representative of Staten Island, I continue to stress the importance of toll equity. Staten Island businesses and residents face some of the worst traffic conditions in the nation. We have the longest average commute times, inconsistent bus transit options and obviously no subway system like our other boroughs. Adding to this nightmare, we are disproportionately impacted by excessive tolls and congestion pricing is no exception. Congestion pricing will financially impact Staten Islanders who commute to the city by car, given the more limited public transportation options available to us. Over the years, I have testified about the urgent need to strengthen Staten Island’s public transportation network. Though some of the projects have come to fruition, many have yet to happen due to a lack of funding. If we expect Staten Islanders to leave their cars at home, we must provide sufficient alternatives and if not enhanced public transportation opportunities, certainly no further tolling. For these reasons, I voted no on the 2019 budget bill to implement this plan.

name: Michael Cusick
comment_text: I am especially concerned for our essential workers who are not exempt under any of the scenarios outlined in the comprehensive report released earlier in August. Many essential workers including firefighters, police officers, doctors, nurses, and others commute from Staten Island to Manhattan at all hours of the day for their shifts.

comment_text: I continue to support an alternative which I have proposed in the past. I support a plan in which Staten Islanders who commute over the Verrazzano Bridge and through the Hugh Carey Tunnel are not tolled additionally when entering the central business district zone.

name: Ed Day
comment_text: Okay. Thank you very much. And my name is County Executive Ed Day. I want to thank you for the opportunity. Unlike almost all of the members of the Metropolitan Community Transportation District, Rockland County has no one-seat rail ride to the Central Business District and severely limited mass transit alternatives. This transit desert forces more than 60 percent of our residents to drive into the city because they have no other way to get there. And that commute is not cheap. Our residents pay heavy tolls on the George Washington Bridge, Lincoln Tunnel and Tappan Zee Bridge for decades, while being subjected to a 40 million-dollar annual value gap between what we pay to the MTA and what we get in return. That equates to a 40 million-dollar gap in just the last decade. And now you want these commuters to give even more while all the East River bridges remain toll free despite the significant transit options to get into the city from those communities. Among those commuters include cops, firefighters and others whose work schedules would leave them stranded if not using their own vehicle. Have all of you forgotten 9/11? Is this your reward for their sacrifice? Connecticut commuters, yes, an entirely different state, do not pay one red cent and unbelievably receive better service from the MTA than our overpaying MTA member Rockland county. One project that's proven this point is the MTA's recent 1.3 billion dollar Penn Station access project to provide a second one-seat extension ride into Penn Station for Metro-North, east of the Hudson commuters. Yes, a premium one-seat ride, while we in Rockland still cannot get that basic one-seat service. In exchange for that $40 million extra collected by the MTA from Rockland each year, our county has received service reduction and increased fares. No improvements to the Pascack Valley rail line in 15 years. And no significant improvements to facilities, rolling stockyards or equipment. Now, the MTA will say they invested heavily into west of the Hudson Port Jervis line, which is true. But unfortunately, that line only serves only one station in Rockland. And our residents make up less than two percent of that ridership. I challenge and invited each and every one of you to find any significant MTA investment that has been made in Rockland County in the last 15 years. Rockland county residents faced by far the highest level of transit inequity in the MTA region, and it would be an insult to these families who are already struggling to keep up with rising gas prices and record-breaking inflation to move this forward without an exemption as part of the CBD Tolling Program if it is implemented. Thank you very much.

organization: Rockland County Office of the County Executive
comment_text: MTA’s lack of investment and “ownership” of its West of Hudson rail service is apparent. It is no secret that Metro-North does not consider itself responsible for the Pascack Valley line trains that serve Rockland County. name: Edwin J. Day
organization: Rockland County Office of the County Executive
comment_text: Since the last formal analyses, Rockland County’s value gap with MTA has unquestionably grown, while other members have seen increased value through MTA’s tremendous capital investments. There have been virtually no capital investments in Rockland County. MTA officials often point to Metro-North’s heavy investment in its West of Hudson Port Jervis line service and infrastructure. Unfortunately, the Port Jervis line serves just one station in Rockland County and our residents make up less than two percent of the ridership on that line. I invite you to review MTA’s Capital Programs over the past 10+ years and challenge you to find any significant investment in Rockland County. In fact, MTA deferred West of Hudson capital investments that should have been made here years ago – investments recommended by MTA’s own 20-Year Needs Assessment. And the 20-Year Needs Assessment currently being developed has not identified any potential expansion or enhancement projects for Rockland County. One of MTA’s investment principles is to “expand network reach” by connecting “underserved or new communities to education and employment opportunities.” Yet Rockland County – a welldocumented underserved community – continues to get pushed to the back of the line.

name: Edwin J. Day
organization: Rockland County Office of the County Executive
comment_text: I acknowledge that the MTA needs a regular source of money for its Capital Program, and that the revenue from the CBD Tolling Program could provide those funds. CBDTP presentations have asserted that investing in an improved mass transit system can help promote equity by providing expanded access to the system. All of this sounds great, if only Rockland County would actually benefit from any of those investments. Rockland County has been seeking equity from the MTA for 35 years. Paying more to the MTA in the form of congestion pricing tolls without any subsequent MTA investment in Rockland County will only serve to increase our value gap exponentially.

name: Jeffrey Dinowitz
comment_text: The Central Business District Tolling Program (CBDTP), better known as congestion pricing, will benefit the greater New York City metropolitan area. While the overall impact of the CBDTP will be positive and will ultimately cause an overall reduction of mobile air toxins across the region, the proposed program increases air pollution within the Bronx. Even as the Bronx has taken steps forward with reducing carbon emissions, this is a step back for the neighborhoods surrounding the Cross Bronx Expressway, due to the increased air pollution from vehicles on the highway. The MTA's report notes an overall decline in air pollution across the city and region, but an increase for the Bronx. This is primarily due to increased vehicle miles traveled on the Cross Bronx Expressway, and the reality is there would be an additional increase on other highways, including the Bruckner Expressway and Major Deegan, through secondary transportation pressure, even if the methodology doesn’t show an increase. The CBDTP is therefore an issue affecting health, equity, and environmental justice issues for the communities we represent, which have historically taken on more than their fair share for decades. In order to have our support for the CBDTP, these Bronx neighborhoods need to see direct benefits that will result in a reduction of mobile air toxins. The best solution would be prioritizing the capital funding for the capping of the Cross Bronx Expressway. Money was allocated as part of the bipartisan infrastructure bill that Senator Chuck Schumer and Congressman Ritchie Torres were both instrumental in getting passed, but the project will need additional resources and it should be prioritized by the city and state. It is also important that the deck on top of the Cross Bronx provide additional long-term benefits, such as providing green space or by creating a public transportation light rail line. This line could provide an east-west railway link stretching from Washington Heights to Parkchester, creating connections across eight subway lines and serving the nearly 600,000 people that live in adjacent neighborhoods. In addition to fully funding the Cross Bronx decking, further priority should be given to projects that would reduce greenhouse gas emissions, such as providing free buses across the entire city, or, at a minimum, within Bronx environmental justice areas harmed by the CBDTP to further incentivize public transportation options for residents that need it the most. The city should also pass electric vehicle supportive legislation that will remove hurdles for where electric vehicle charging stations can be located and provide opportunities for electric vehicle investment across the city. This will encourage the transition to electric vehicles, which will be key to reducing emissions within the city. Other ways the city can support these environmental justice areas include prioritizing and further incentivizing renewable energy bonuses for building upgrades. The Bronx has many buildings with low-income residents and the city needs to support improvements to these buildings in order for building upgrades to happen. For NYCHA buildings, the city needs to prioritize and fully fund renewable energy upgrades. OFFICE OF THE BRONX BOROUGH PRESIDENT - 851 GRAND CONCOURSE, SUITE 301, BRONX, NY 10451 - (718) 590-3500

With the CBDTP adding to that historical burden, it is time the Bronx receives major capital improvements that will provide real health benefits in these environmental justice communities. name: Simcha Eichenstein
comment_text: We are writing to ask that you withdraw your support for the Metropolitan Transportation Authority’s (MTA) “Central Business District Tolling Program.”

name: Simcha Eichenstein
comment_text: The Environmental Assessment (EA) released by the MTA on August 10th makes it clear that the only objectives of the Central Business District Tolling Program (CBD) are to 1) reduce the miles vehicles travel within Central Manhattan by five percent; 2) reduce the number of cars coming into Central Manhattan by 10 percent; and 3) create a significant new funding source for the MTA. To create this marginal traffic benefit to Manhattan residents living within the proposed central business district, the CBD tolling program would charge an exorbitant toll for driving, which would effectively redisperse traffic congestion across other parts of New York City and the tri-state area, rather than reducing overall traffic. This toll, along with the negative environmental and financial impacts of this increased traffic in their communities, would disproportionately harm low and middle-income outer borough residents. Furthermore, at no point does the EA provide any conclusive evidence that this program would provide a source of revenue that is a stable and sustainable, nor does the MTA commit to specifically improving public transportation in areas of the city where it is significantly lacking.

name: Simcha Eichenstein
comment_text: Once again, we should look to London, where the clogged main and arterial roadways across the city have had a particularly deleterious impact on communities outside the congestion pricing zone. Spillover traffic and motorists trying to avoid congestion now take circuitous routes through residential areas across the city and in neighborhoods in Outer London – what locals pejoratively call “rat running.” Rat running has led to traffic in otherwise quiet, arterial roads to double in the decade between 2009 and 2019, according to DfT data. The problem has gotten so bad that many borough officials began taking matters into their own hands, embarking on a new car-reduction plan called Low Traffic Neighborhoods by erecting barriers to prevent outside motorists from using their streets. The EA supports this:

name: Simcha Eichenstein
comment_text: • Those travelling outside the CBD will see no reduction, and likely higher traffic volumes, despite the overwhelming number of New Yorkers who face congestion in Brooklyn, Queens, Staten Island, the Bronx, Nassau, on Long Island, the Hudson Valley, New Jersey, and Connecticut. In fact, even the optimistic data within the EA, shows traffic overall getting worse for Long Island, New Jersey, and Connecticut. In sum, the people who will pay the price get worse traffic. (Table ES-4) Mid-day and PM traffic volumes approaching the westbound George Washington Bridge will result in additional traffic throughout its northern Manhattan and South Bronx approaches. (4B-21) The EA estimates this will double pedestrian volume at already overcrowded NYC Subway stations in and around the central business district. (Table ES-4) The CBD Tolling Program Could Have Disastrous Health Impacts

name: Simcha Eichenstein
comment_text: Even so, these estimates are troubling, especially when you look at the effect London’s congestion pricing has had on air pollution in Outer London and its suburbs over the last two decades. The toxic air pollution being caused by the increased traffic there is leading to nearly 4,000 premature deaths a year and children being born at lower birthweight, stunted lungs, and higher incidences of asthma, according to a recent study by the Imperial College of London. The CBD Tolling Program is a Regressive Tax

name: Simcha Eichenstein
comment_text: Other concerning EA findings: • In every scenario, Staten Island will see more congestion from personal vehicles and trucks on highways and local streets. (Table 4A-25 & 4A-26) • In every alternative, the Bronx will see more traffic from thousands of additional commercial trucks, and in almost every scenario, the Bronx will see more traffic from personal vehicles. (Table 4A-28 &4A-29) Most of this additional traffic will be on the Cross Bronx Expressway, which has the distinction of having some of the worst asthma health outcomes in the nation. This tolling program will have little impact on the day-to-day life of wealthy commuters or residents within the Manhattan CBD. But the vast majority of the 1,856,000 people who enter the CBD by car each day – working- and middle-class residents of the outer boroughs and suburbs - and will now be forced to pay for these fortunate few. That is far greater than the entire population and beneficiaries living within the CBD. (EA Page 1-13). Even the EA begrudgingly admits, this toll would disproportionately impact on low-income New Yorkers, making this program a new regressive tax. (Table ES-4). Other EA findings:

name: Simcha Eichenstein
comment_text: • The amount of total vehicle miles traveled throughout the 28-county study area will be reduced by between 0.2% and 0.4% by implementing any of the tolling scenarios as compared to taking no action, and by 2045, that number will only climb to a maximum of 0.5% at best. Meaning, it is a $1 billion annual tax on the region, without any regional benefit. (Table 4A-6, 4A-7 & 4A-14) The increase in daily commuting costs for auto drivers from New York City outside of the CBD will range from 7.9% to 37.2%, most significantly impacting lower income and minority drivers. Increases to Long Island, Hudson Valley, New Jersey, and Connecticut drivers will range from 5.8% to 26.5% (Table 4A-18) Drivers from New York City outside of the CBD can possibly face total daily tolls of up to $38.20, with the tolls having a disproportionate effect on lowincome families (Table 4A-19) No alternatives to generate $1 billion in revenue other than car-related fees were considered by the MTA that could spread the cost out more equitable and progressively through the regional population. name: Sruly Eisenbach
organization: Trustee Village of Spring Valley, Rockland County
comment_text: With respect to the CBD toll being a new tax, unlike a new tax, the proposed CBD toll would not apply to everyone. Rather, it would apply to people who drive into or out of the Manhattan CBD. Transit riders already have a cost associated with their travel to the Manhattan CBD since they must pay a fare to use the service, but these costs are not currently paid by drivers using certain routes. A toll to enter the Manhattan CBD for drivers is like the user fee (fare) paid by transit riders. Consistent with the Traffic Mobility Act, MTA would use the net revenue generated by the CBD Tolling Program to fund transit and commuter rail projects in the MTA 2020–2024 Capital Program and successor programs. Ten percent of the net revenues would be allocated to investments in Metro-North Railroad, which provides service in Rockland County. The CBDTP would improve travel conditions in Manhattan for all travelers to the Manhattan CBD by reducing peak-hour traffic entering and leaving the City. All vehicle operators in Manhattan would benefit from reduced travel times and reduced fuel consumption, which importantly includes Rockland drivers who visit and work in New York. Revenues invested in maintaining and enhancing NYCT buses and subways would also benefit those from Rockland County traveling throughout the City via public transit. See also responses to Frequently Received Comment 4, Frequently Received Comment 18, and Frequently Received Comment 23.

comment_text: Okay. Well, thank you for taking the time to do all these hearings. And to -- to really focus on the needs of New York City. My district is entirely within the congestion zone, and I voted for congestion pricing and I support this moving forward. I think it's critical now that we need to deal with the traffic and the environmental crisis we are living in right now. I really urge you to consider a few things as you move forward through this, and things that we had understood when we voted on this legislation. One is around the time period and really stagger out the cost related to rush hour and non-rush hour traffic. There's a lot -- I hear a lot of talk from constituents who live in the district. They're going away. Potentially they may have a vehicle and they're leaving on the weekend.
