We should -- whatever tolling you put together for congestion pricing should really reflect that reality. In addition, we've heard a lot about parking outside the congestion zone and that people may end up parking in Brooklyn or above 60th Street in Manhattan. And we really need to think about ways to avoid people trying to park, quote, for free on the street with alternative side parking outside of the congestion zone in an attempt to avoid it. I will work on and encourage you to look at residential parking as a tool to combat that problem. I really believe that congestion pricing will reduce the traffic flow into Manhattan and hopefully reduce the traffic flow around the city. name: Harvey Epstein
comment_text: Conclusion Traffic congestion costs billions of dollars. Congestion pricing lessens congestion. Behind the dollar costs of traffic congestion are frustrations, inefficiencies and even tragedies: wasted time, missed appointments, deadly crashes and pollution. We don’t have a lot of time to address the problems caused by traffic congestion, specifically pollution. We established a goal in the Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act to reduce our greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by at least 85% below 1990-level GHG emissions by 2050. I believe congestion pricing will help us meet that critical goal while also reducing the other negative effects of traffic congestion. Thank you for the opportunity to submit comments. Traffic congestion contributes to poor air quality, increased risk of crashes, noise pollution, and wasted time. When quantified, the costs of these negative impacts are in the billions of dollars. name: Harvey Epstein
comment_text: Resident Exemptions The MTA Reform and Traffic Mobility Act provided for an exemption for central business district residents earning less than $60,000 a year in the form of a tax credit. A uniform exemption at $60,000 is a regressive solution, especially for lower income families compared to a household of one. We must reduce the burden on low-income residents who for whatever reason need to keep a car and drive. The difference in ability to pay tolls between an individual earning $60,000 and a family of four earning $60,000 is obvious. A resident exemption should be based on area median income, which is a more practical way to measure income in this context. Remember, this new law will charge people who live in the congestion zone who are just going home when they drive. In addition, Waterside Plaza is outside the congestion zone so driving to Waterside Plaza from the FDR should be excluded from the congestion pricing plan since the development is not to the west of the FDR as outlined in our legislation. Time Periods The toll should be variable based on the hours where traffic is traditionally the worst during rush hours Monday through Friday and vehicles that enter. However, residents leaving the central business district on evenings and weekends do not increase the type congestion the project targets––tolls should reflect that. Parking Congestion pricing will affect parking conditions. With some commuters opting not to drive into the central business district to avoid the toll, parking conditions may improve within the district. However, some commuters may choose to park their vehicles outside the district boundary and then enter the district by another mode of transit, shrinking parking availability for residents outside of the district. To avoid that, the effects of the ongoing provision of free parking to nonresidents should be re-evaluated and we should look toward passing residential park rules for at least Manhattan or NYC as a whole. name: Amanda Farias
comment_text: CO-CHAIR WOMEN’S CAUCUS September 9, 2022 Testimony of Council Member Amanda Farias on the MTA Congestion Pricing Environmental Assessment I began my career as an organizer, advocating for community investments, transit equity, environmental justice, healthcare access and economic stability. First and foremost, I am a lifelong resident of this district, and I, along with my neighbors, have suffered from disinvestment in the Bronx that resulted in negative health implications like asthma, higher expenses due to lack of transit infrastructure, and slow economic progress. The Environmental Assessment the MTA conducted only proves the disregard for the Bronx and its residents continues with alarming findings that will negatively impact communities like mine. Page ES-3 of the Executive Summary describes the need for an environmental assessment and clearly states that, “the approach to reducing congestion in Manhattan Central Business District (CBD) lends itself to beneficial effects on air quality and quality of life.” But what is not included in this simplified analysis is that these benefits are subjective to where you live. In New York City we already know that where you live is based primarily on socio-economic status.

name: Amanda Farias
comment_text: Those living in Manhattan are often of financial privilege, especially with rent continuing to rise drastically each year. According to a Douglas Elliman report, the average rent in Manhattan rose to $5,058 in June 2022, up from $4,975 in May and $3,922 in June 2021. In order to pay that rent alone, with no other costs included, one would have to make around $29 an hour. Even with this salary, which is almost double our current minimum wage, you would not be able to afford food, public transit, or any other living expenses. According to the latest census data the Bronx per capita income is $22,749 a year, which equals $11 an hour. I am sharing this data to highlight the very real and major economic disparities that exist across the different boroughs of New York City. My concern is that these disparities will only be exacerbated by the increased congestion this plan is bringing to the Bronx due to rerouting of drivers to avoid the new tolls. This plan disrupts economic justice for many hard working New Yorkers. My district is home to thousands of For-Hire Vehicle (FHV) drivers and taxi drivers - both of which have paid congestion fees to the MTA since 2019. The Bronx is also home to around 45% of Lyft drivers who have already been paying a fee, which has brought in over $1 billion in revenue for the MTA since 2019. Most of whom are immigrant, Black and Brown New Yorkers. The new proposed fee structure would allow a person taking a trip within Manhattan to pay nothing, while someone from my district, or someone who lives in another outer-borough Thinking about the economic justice aspect of this program, we also need to think pragmatically about the many essential workers, CUNY students, veterans, people on fixed income, and those with major financial constraints from being charged a $20+ fee. Economically, there may need to be considerations for exemptions or discounts to the fees proposed for specific criteria of New Yorkers. Traffic congestion and air pollution are a major concern in the outer boroughs and we do urgently need policy and infrastructure plans that actively prioritizes healing the decades of neglect many of our Black and Brown communities have dealt with. The CBDTP in its current form does not accomplish this.

name: Amanda Farias
comment_text: It is obvious that the MTA needs funding to make critical infrastructure upgrades, such as increasing ADA compliance through elevator installation, and the larger scale of citywide transit infrastructure investments needs, like capping the Cross Bronx Expressway. However, this plan does too much harm to the South Bronx - a community who is already suffering from decades of environmental racism. For this program to be successful we need to be proactive about the outlined environmental impacts CBDTP will have on our South Bronx communities. I strongly urge the MTA to work with our counterparts at all levels of government to finally pursue the project to cap the Cross Bronx Expressway, work on air quality mitigants, determine areas to hinder the trucks from utilizing the Cross Bronx, and other ways to be innovative if support from the Bronx Delegation on CBDTP is desired. I am here to work with the agency to figure out how to incentivize use of public transportation in an equitable way that prioritizes our Black and Brown communities in the outer-boroughs.

name: Amanda Farias
comment_text: As the Chair of the Committee on Economic Development, I feel it is critical that we make sure to support our essential workers and improve access to good quality jobs in this City. name: Amanda Farias
comment_text: The Central Business District Tolling Program (CBDTP), better known as congestion pricing, will benefit the greater New York City metropolitan area. While the overall impact of the CBDTP will be positive and will ultimately cause an overall reduction of mobile air toxins across the region, the proposed program increases air pollution within the Bronx. Even as the Bronx has taken steps forward with reducing carbon emissions, this is a step back for the neighborhoods surrounding the Cross Bronx Expressway, due to the increased air pollution from vehicles on the highway. The MTA's report notes an overall decline in air pollution across the city and region, but an increase for the Bronx. This is primarily due to increased vehicle miles traveled on the Cross Bronx Expressway, and the reality is there would be an additional increase on other highways, including the Bruckner Expressway and Major Deegan, through secondary transportation pressure, even if the methodology doesn’t show an increase. The CBDTP is therefore an issue affecting health, equity, and environmental justice issues for the communities we represent, which have historically taken on more than their fair share for decades. In order to have our support for the CBDTP, these Bronx neighborhoods need to see direct benefits that will result in a reduction of mobile air toxins. The best solution would be prioritizing the capital funding for the capping of the Cross Bronx Expressway. Money was allocated as part of the bipartisan infrastructure bill that Senator Chuck Schumer and Congressman Ritchie Torres were both instrumental in getting passed, but the project will need additional resources and it should be prioritized by the city and state. It is also important that the deck on top of the Cross Bronx provide additional long-term benefits, such as providing green space or by creating a public transportation light rail line. This line could provide an east-west railway link stretching from Washington Heights to Parkchester, creating connections across eight subway lines and serving the nearly 600,000 people that live in adjacent neighborhoods. In addition to fully funding the Cross Bronx decking, further priority should be given to projects that would reduce greenhouse gas emissions, such as providing free buses across the entire city, or, at a minimum, within Bronx environmental justice areas harmed by the CBDTP to further incentivize public transportation options for residents that need it the most. The city should also pass electric vehicle supportive legislation that will remove hurdles for where electric vehicle charging stations can be located and provide opportunities for electric vehicle investment across the city. This will encourage the transition to electric vehicles, which will be key to reducing emissions within the city. Other ways the city can support these environmental justice areas include prioritizing and further incentivizing renewable energy bonuses for building upgrades. The Bronx has many buildings with low-income residents and the city needs to support improvements to these buildings in order for building upgrades to happen. For NYCHA buildings, the city needs to prioritize and fully fund renewable energy upgrades. OFFICE OF THE BRONX BOROUGH PRESIDENT - 851 GRAND CONCOURSE, SUITE 301, BRONX, NY 10451 - (718) 590-3500

comment_text: ST September 9, 2022 Honorable Kathy Hochul Governor State of New York 633 3rd Ave 38th floor New York, NY 10017 Dear Governor Hochul:

name: Simcha Felder
comment_text: We are writing to ask that you withdraw your support for the Metropolitan Transportation Authority’s (MTA) “Central Business District Tolling Program.”

name: Simcha Felder
comment_text: The Environmental Assessment (EA) released by the MTA on August 10th makes it clear that the only objectives of the Central Business District Tolling Program (CBD) are to 1) reduce the miles vehicles travel within Central Manhattan by five percent; 2) reduce the number of cars coming into Central Manhattan by 10 percent; and 3) create a significant new funding source for the MTA. To create this marginal traffic benefit to Manhattan residents living within the proposed central business district, the CBD tolling program would charge an exorbitant toll for driving, which would effectively redisperse traffic congestion across other parts of New York City and the tri-state area, rather than reducing overall traffic. This toll, along with the negative environmental and financial impacts of this increased traffic in their communities, would disproportionately harm low and middle-income outer borough residents. Furthermore, at no point does the EA provide any conclusive evidence that this program would provide a source of revenue that is a stable and sustainable, nor does the MTA commit to specifically improving public transportation in areas of the city where it is significantly lacking.

name: Simcha Felder
comment_text: Once again, we should look to London, where the clogged main and arterial roadways across the city have had a particularly deleterious impact on communities outside the congestion pricing zone. Spillover traffic and motorists trying to avoid congestion now take circuitous routes through residential areas across the city and in neighborhoods in Outer London – what locals pejoratively call “rat running.” Rat running has led to traffic in otherwise quiet, arterial roads to double in the decade between 2009 and 2019, according to DfT data. The problem has gotten so bad that many borough officials began taking matters into their own hands, embarking on a new car-reduction plan called Low Traffic Neighborhoods by erecting barriers to prevent outside motorists from using their streets. The EA supports this:

name: Simcha Felder
comment_text: • Those travelling outside the CBD will see no reduction, and likely higher traffic volumes, despite the overwhelming number of New Yorkers who face congestion in Brooklyn, Queens, Staten Island, the Bronx, Nassau, on Long Island, the Hudson Valley, New Jersey, and Connecticut. In fact, even the optimistic data within the EA, shows traffic overall getting worse for Long Island, New Jersey, and Connecticut. In sum, the people who will pay the price get worse traffic. (Table ES-4) Mid-day and PM traffic volumes approaching the westbound George Washington Bridge will result in additional traffic throughout its northern Manhattan and South Bronx approaches. (4B-21) The EA estimates this will double pedestrian volume at already overcrowded NYC Subway stations in and around the central business district. (Table ES-4) The CBD Tolling Program Could Have Disastrous Health Impacts

name: Simcha Felder
comment_text: Even so, these estimates are troubling, especially when you look at the effect London’s congestion pricing has had on air pollution in Outer London and its suburbs over the last two decades. The toxic air pollution being caused by the increased traffic there is leading to nearly 4,000 premature deaths a year and children being born at lower birthweight, stunted lungs, and higher incidences of asthma, according to a recent study by the Imperial College of London. The CBD Tolling Program is a Regressive Tax

name: Simcha Felder
comment_text: Other concerning EA findings: • In every scenario, Staten Island will see more congestion from personal vehicles and trucks on highways and local streets. (Table 4A-25 & 4A-26) • In every alternative, the Bronx will see more traffic from thousands of additional commercial trucks, and in almost every scenario, the Bronx will see more traffic from personal vehicles. (Table 4A-28 &4A-29) Most of this additional traffic will be on the Cross Bronx Expressway, which has the distinction of having some of the worst asthma health outcomes in the nation. This tolling program will have little impact on the day-to-day life of wealthy commuters or residents within the Manhattan CBD. But the vast majority of the 1,856,000 people who enter the CBD by car each day – working- and middle-class residents of the outer boroughs and suburbs - and will now be forced to pay for these fortunate few. That is far greater than the entire population and beneficiaries living within the CBD. (EA Page 1-13). Even the EA begrudgingly admits, this toll would disproportionately impact on low-income New Yorkers, making this program a new regressive tax. (Table ES-4). Other EA findings:

name: Simcha Felder
comment_text: • The amount of total vehicle miles traveled throughout the 28-county study area will be reduced by between 0.2% and 0.4% by implementing any of the tolling scenarios as compared to taking no action, and by 2045, that number will only climb to a maximum of 0.5% at best. Meaning, it is a $1 billion annual tax on the region, without any regional benefit. (Table 4A-6, 4A-7 & 4A-14) The increase in daily commuting costs for auto drivers from New York City outside of the CBD will range from 7.9% to 37.2%, most significantly impacting lower income and minority drivers. Increases to Long Island, Hudson Valley, New Jersey, and Connecticut drivers will range from 5.8% to 26.5% (Table 4A-18) Drivers from New York City outside of the CBD can possibly face total daily tolls of up to $38.20, with the tolls having a disproportionate effect on lowincome families (Table 4A-19) No alternatives to generate $1 billion in revenue other than car-related fees were considered by the MTA that could spread the cost out more equitable and progressively through the regional population. The EA estimates the CBD Tolling Program would increase dangerous atmospheric pollutants – particulate matter, nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide, and volatile organic compounds – for Staten Island and the Bronx (Table 10-8). Considering the predicted increases in spillover traffic, particularly the hundreds of new trucks expected to fill the roads in these boroughs each hour, these estimates are laughably low and defy common sense (Table ES-4). Congestion Pricing Is Not a Budget Unicorn

name: Simcha Felder
comment_text: Congestion charge payments in London accounted for £232m (about $275 million) in revenue in 2021, or less than four percent of the total revenue for Transport for London (TfL), the city’s public transportation agency. Those figures came in after Mayor Sadiq Kahn increased the daily rate from £11.50 to £15 ($13 to $17.75) and adjusted the operating hours to includes 6PM-10PM and weekends to try to boost the agency’s income. The city’s congestion charge has failed to generate enough revenue to help TfL survive a precipitous drop in ridership and an economic downturn. The agency recently needed a $6 billion bailout from the federal government just to stay afloat. Considering London’s significantly higher traffic volumes, there is no chance the CBD Tolling Program would come close to generating the $1 billion MTA is projecting in the EA – especially when that figure does not incorporate exemptions that are being considered for New Jersey drivers, for-hire vehicles, and others. Given the MTA’s long, notorious history of fiscal mismanagement, cost-overruns, and failures to meet even the most generous project deadlines, it is simply magical

name: Simcha Felder
comment_text: Given all of these factors, to say that the Central Business District Tolling Program is problematic is an understatement: It is a disaster waiting to happen. We cannot in good conscience support a project that would be so harmful to so many New York City residents, and as leader of this state, we urge you to reconsider. Thank you for your time, courtesy, and consideration. Very truly yours, Joseph C. name: Shmuli Fromovitz
organization: Trustee Village of Chestnut Ridge, Rockland County
comment_text: We are a group of concerned elected officials in Rockland County. We write to you in opposition of the current plan to charge Rockland County residents with the new congestion pricing, and we are putting forth our request that Rockland County residents be exempt from paying this surcharge. Unlike our neighbors east of the Hudson who have nearly 45 train stations, we in Rockland County have only 5 stations, none of which have trains going directly into Manhattan. Until the transit access to the city is vastly improved, congestion pricing will amount to an unfair tax to subsidize a transit system that does not equitably serve our community. Our residents will be charged thousands of dollars per year for their drive into the city without having a convenient transit alternative. For the past decade, we were forced to subsidize mass transit for the rest of our region as we contributed millions of dollars annually -- far more than the MTA invests into our County.

name: Shmuli Fromovitz
organization: Trustee Village of Chestnut Ridge, Rockland County
comment_text: The complete disregard of the residents who live West of the Hudson has been evident in every step of the congestion pricing plan as we don’t even have a voice at the table when decisions are made on these matters. Therefore, we urge you to exempt Rockland County residents from congestion pricing as long as there is no viable one seat ride option into Manhattan. Thank you for your consideration of this matter. name: Shmuli Fromovitz
organization: Trustee Village of Chestnut Ridge, Rockland County
comment_text: With respect to the CBD toll being a new tax, unlike a new tax, the proposed CBD toll would not apply to everyone. Rather, it would apply to people who drive into or out of the Manhattan CBD. Transit riders already have a cost associated with their travel to the Manhattan CBD since they must pay a fare to use the service, but these costs are not currently paid by drivers using certain routes. A toll to enter the Manhattan CBD for drivers is like the user fee (fare) paid by transit riders. Consistent with the Traffic Mobility Act, MTA would use the net revenue generated by the CBD Tolling Program to fund transit and commuter rail projects in the MTA 2020–2024 Capital Program and successor programs. Ten percent of the net revenues would be allocated to investments in Metro-North Railroad, which provides service in Rockland County. The CBDTP would improve travel conditions in Manhattan for all travelers to the Manhattan CBD by reducing peak-hour traffic entering and leaving the City. All vehicle operators in Manhattan would benefit from reduced travel times and reduced fuel consumption, which importantly includes Rockland drivers who visit and work in New York. Revenues invested in maintaining and enhancing NYCT buses and subways would also benefit those from Rockland County traveling throughout the City via public transit. See also responses to Frequently Received Comment 4, Frequently Received Comment 18, and Frequently Received Comment 23.

comment_text: The Central Business District Tolling Program (CBDTP), better known as congestion pricing, will benefit the greater New York City metropolitan area. While the overall impact of the CBDTP will be positive and will ultimately cause an overall reduction of mobile air toxins across the region, the proposed program increases air pollution within the Bronx. Even as the Bronx has taken steps forward with reducing carbon emissions, this is a step back for the neighborhoods surrounding the Cross Bronx Expressway, due to the increased air pollution from vehicles on the highway. The MTA's report notes an overall decline in air pollution across the city and region, but an increase for the Bronx. This is primarily due to increased vehicle miles traveled on the Cross Bronx Expressway, and the reality is there would be an additional increase on other highways, including the Bruckner Expressway and Major Deegan, through secondary transportation pressure, even if the methodology doesn’t show an increase. The CBDTP is therefore an issue affecting health, equity, and environmental justice issues for the communities we represent, which have historically taken on more than their fair share for decades. In order to have our support for the CBDTP, these Bronx neighborhoods need to see direct benefits that will result in a reduction of mobile air toxins. The best solution would be prioritizing the capital funding for the capping of the Cross Bronx Expressway. Money was allocated as part of the bipartisan infrastructure bill that Senator Chuck Schumer and Congressman Ritchie Torres were both instrumental in getting passed, but the project will need additional resources and it should be prioritized by the city and state. It is also important that the deck on top of the Cross Bronx provide additional long-term benefits, such as providing green space or by creating a public transportation light rail line. This line could provide an east-west railway link stretching from Washington Heights to Parkchester, creating connections across eight subway lines and serving the nearly 600,000 people that live in adjacent neighborhoods. In addition to fully funding the Cross Bronx decking, further priority should be given to projects that would reduce greenhouse gas emissions, such as providing free buses across the entire city, or, at a minimum, within Bronx environmental justice areas harmed by the CBDTP to further incentivize public transportation options for residents that need it the most. The city should also pass electric vehicle supportive legislation that will remove hurdles for where electric vehicle charging stations can be located and provide opportunities for electric vehicle investment across the city. This will encourage the transition to electric vehicles, which will be key to reducing emissions within the city. comment_text: I am concerned with the current proposal to charge FHVs the full congestion pricing toll each time they enter the zone. A system designed specifically for FHVs already charges each rider a set pertrip fee for rides south of 96th Street. This fee is charged directly to the rider rather than to the driver of the FHV. There are no plans to remove the per-trip fee under the CBDTP proposal, resulting in a double congestion fee for each ride into the CBD toll area. The current FHV per-trip fee generates approximately $400 million annually for the MTA. Additionally, I am concerned that the proposed CBD fare structure does not work well with FHVs because it would allow a person taking a trip within the CBD fare area to pay nothing, whereas someone getting a ride that crosses the CBD toll area would be expected to pay. Even if there is only a once-per-day CBD fare for FHVs, the fee would be charged either to the driver or to the first pick-up that crosses the CBD each day. Drivers incurring a congestion pricing fee would force them to pay to complete a passenger’s ride from their earnings, which will cause undue hardship to an already struggling industry. I am a proud supporter of the tens of thousands of drivers who work tirelessly to provide FHV and taxi services, many of whom live in The Bronx. It is crucial that we support the drivers working to provide transportation options to New Yorkers, and, to do this, we must be sure that the program does not cause undue harm to these working people. I believe it is possible to create a CBDTP model that accomplishes the dual goals of reducing congestion and raising revenue while not unduly harming these drivers. A potential compromise is to continue with the current FHV model which has established a fee structure that is charged directly to the rider for each ride. name: Deborah Glick
comment_text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify before you today regarding the MTA's plan for the CBD Tolling Program. The need to reduce gas emissions and create a reliable revenue stream to improve our transit system makes congestion pricing a reasonable policy choice. There is a need to improve accessibility for people with disabilities, upgrade critical infrastructure, move buses towards zero emissions and improve subway safety. However, in regards to the implementation of this project, there are a few concerns I have about the residents who live in the CBD and how this will impact their lives. My first concern is about how this will impact the economy. It is reasonable to assume that everyone in the congestion zone will experience passalong charges for services and deliveries, unlike New Yorkers living uptown or anywhere outside of the CBD. The promised impact of the program on the environment is still hypothetical, but the impact it will have on hundreds of thousands of residents' pocketbooks, many of whom are struggling economically as it is, is certain. Whether they own a car or not. While it is viewed as harsh by many people in the congestion zone to be charged an extra fee simply to drive home, it seems especially punitive to charge them to leave home, which the remaining in zone toll seems to do. The ancillary impact of new tolls put a severe burden on our residents, most of whom do not contribute to the congestion or pollution, considering that the majority of them either do not have cars or leave their cars parked in already heavily taxed parking meter zones or parking garage. However, those who do use vehicles due to medical treatments may be especially disadvantaged. Another concern is how the tolls will impact God's Love We Deliver, a not-for-profit based in the CBD, which will experience an estimated cost of half a million dollars a year to continue to serve historically marginalized communities, and where 90 percent of their clients are below the poverty line. An exemption or a discount for this critical service is a top priority, as it will surely affect the lives of New Yorkers who need these services to survive and live in all parts of the city. In closing, I reiterate my support for congestion pricing, and understand that the committee has said any consideration in one area increases the need for higher tolls to cover that consideration. But I suggest that solely relying on congestion pricing to cover the MTA needs may not be the most equitable solution and an added additional broad-based revenue stream should be considered. Thank you.

It is essential that we improve accessibility for people with disabilities, upgrade critical infrastructure, move buses toward zero emissions and improve subway safety. However, with respect to the implementation of this program, I have concerns about the residents who live in the CBD zone and how this will impact their lives. My first concern is about the financial impact of those who reside or own small businesses in the CBD zone and the ability of people to remain in our communities because of that direct impact to the local economy. For individuals who drive cars for work, or to receive regular medical treatments and do not have a low income enough to qualify for a waiver, this may be an impossible burden, especially for those who are already struggling with fixed or modest incomes. It is reasonable to assume that everyone residing or doing business in the congestion zone will experience pass-along charges for services and deliveries, unlike New Yorkers living uptown, or anywhere outside of the CBD. The promised impact of the program on the environment is still hypothetical, but the impact it will have on hundreds of thousands of residents’ pocketbooks is certain, whether or not they own a car. Since there is no time of day or night when the congestion fee can be avoided, it is viewed as harsh by many people living in the congestion zone to be charged an extra fee simply to drive home. It appears that this might trigger a fee to leave the zone. That nebulous phrase needs clarification, because it would be especially punitive to charge residents to leave home, as well as charge them to return home. The ancillary impact of new tolls puts a severe burden on our residents, particularly since most do not contribute to the congestion or pollution, as the majority of them either do not have cars or leave their cars parked in already heavily taxed parking-metered areas or parking garages. name: Richard Gottfried
comment_text: I am Assembly Member Richard N. Gottfried. I represent New York’s 75th Assembly District, which includes much of the Manhattan Central Business District (CBD) as defined by the MTA’s Central Business District Tolling Program. I support the concept and implementation of congestion pricing and voted for the legislation authorizing its implementation. Congestion pricing will enable New York City to improve air quality, street safety, quality of life, and public transit; and reduce traffic congestion and noise. Congestion pricing will raise crucial funds for the MTA to increase mass transit accessibility, modernize our transit system, and upgrade trains, systems and buses. Today I reiterate my support for congestion pricing, with several recommendations. New York’s landmark Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act sets goals to reduce emissions of greenhouse gasses that contribute to climate change. The CBD tolling program will help the State reach those goals.

name: Richard Gottfried
comment_text: Under the congestion pricing legislation, all residents of the CBD earning $60,000 annually or less and subject to the toll are to be provided tax rebates to offset the additional costs of traveling in their vehicles. In London’s congestion pricing system, all residents of the affected zone pay a reduced congestion pricing fee. However, creating such a broad exemption or reduction would be costly to the MTA, and would include many high-income New Yorkers who can easily afford the fees. Instead, I favor the more equitable approach advanced by my Assembly colleague, Harvey Epstein, whose legislation (A. 6598) would exempt all residents of the CBD with incomes at or below 120% of the Area Median Income. For a single earner, this would be an annual income of about $100,300 dollars. I am concerned that the proposed system of using tax credits for low-income residents would not work well. Low- and moderate-income people cannot afford to pay the toll up front and wait up to a year for their refund. There should be a mechanism to have the tolling system recognize their vehicles and not impose the toll, or delay imposing the toll until the tax credit is received. As is mandated by the authorizing legislation, I support a toll exemption for all emergency vehicles, and vehicles transporting people with disabilities. In particular, attention needs to be paid to how the board will identify when a disabled person is riding in a vehicle that they may not regularly ride in. I urge the review board to consult with New York City disability rights organizations to ensure equitable implementation of this requirement. Other vehicles to include are vehicles that are transporting people with temporary disabilities and those that respond to emergencies but are not classified as emergency vehicles, such as American Red Cross vehicles which are dispatched from within the congestion zone. My district has some of the highest levels of air pollution in the entire city according to city data. Fine particulate matter (PM2.5), the most harmful urban air pollutant, is most prevalent in the CBD. The particles are small enough to penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, which can worsen lung and heart disease and lead to hospital admissions and premature deaths. It is also known to cause cancer. Vehicle emissions are a central source of this dangerous pollutant in our district. The CBD is also plagued by street safety issues. Intense congestion and misallocation of street space between vehicles, bicycles and pedestrians too often result in injury and death. A reduction in congestion will result in greater ability for the City to design safer and more equitable streets and reduce dangerous incidents. I urge the Traffic Mobility Review Board to consult with the local community boards in the affected areas and along the borders of the CBD regarding the siting and location of gantries on which toll cameras will be mounted. Existing street furniture, such as light poles, should be used as much as possible to reduce taking additional sidewalk space. All care should be taken not to impact street trees.

name: Richard Gottfried
comment_text: The health, safety, and climate impacts of congestion in the city, combined with economic losses due to congestion, and the MTA’s continual financial crises underline the urgency with which we must move to implement this program. Thank you for offering this opportunity to submit comments on the MTA’s Central Business District Tolling Program. I support the concept of “surge pricing” or variable pricing, under which higher tolls are levied during periods of busiest traffic, such as the height of the morning and evening rush hours. Annual time period adjustment is the most equitable way to implement surge pricing as it is predictable. As many residents of the CBD commute out of the area during peak hours, reducing local congestion, pricing should be higher for those entering the zone than those leaving during those periods. The program should also collect variable fees based on the weight and size of vehicles and their level of emissions. Surge pricing through higher fees for certain vehicles can be a useful tool to recoup these funds, and further reduce congestion and pollution on our streets. comment_text:  The MTA also admits that the “toll could reduce taxi and FHV revenues” and – under certain scenarios – that it would have “high and adverse effects [on] taxi and FHV drivers.” The Authority’s response – at a time of a taxi driver suicide epidemic – is to help a few of them find new employment. Instead of trying to help these hard-working people keep their jobs so they can feed their families, the MTA asks them to switch careers without even considering the price of cars and medallions these drivers invested in. This also disrespects their livelihood.  Furthermore, the MTA argues that despite the increased delivery costs caused by the Congestion Tax, it “would not result in changes in the cost of most consumer goods.” This is highly dubious and the MTA should listen to the community groups that testified during the Congestion Tax hearings about how it would raise the costs of fresh fruits and vegetables and medicines.  The Authority also offers no mitigations for “changes in parking demand near the 60th St. CBD boundary” or for the projected increase in vehicle miles traveled (VMT) in Long Island and New Jersey.  Increased truck traffic diversions into poor and low-income neighborhoods are addressed only with monitoring and a gesture at an existing push to electrify buses. The MTA also admits that the Congestion Tax “may produce increased congestion on highway segments approaching circumferential roadways used to avoid CBD tolls, resulting in increased delays and queues in midday and PM peak hours.” The only mitigation offered is monitoring with a vague description of “alternative measures” being possible. Dear Secretary Buttigieg and Acting Administrator Pollack:

name: Josh Gottheimer
comment_text: We are writing to express concern about New York’s looming Congestion Tax. This is a first-in-thenation program that, by the Metropolitan Transportation Authority’s (MTA) own admission, will disproportionately hurt those from low-income and marginalized communities. Therefore, we urge you please to require a complete Environmental Impact Statement (EIS), which the circumstances clearly warrant. This new Congestion Tax would cost New Jersey and New York drivers up to $23 dollars a day — more than $5,000 a year — on top of the already far-too-high $16-a-day tolls for our bridges and tunnels, just to drive south of 60th Street to work in New York City. Unlike the century-old cooperation over shared Port Authority revenues, not a cent will go back to the PATH or NJ Transit to actually help our state in any way. My Office found that seventy-four percent of people who testified at New York’s recent public hearings on the Congestion Tax opposed the program. They are concerned it will lead to more congestion and pollution in their neighborhoods and hurt marginalized communities, health care workers, labor, taxi and FHV drivers, and small businesses. The hearings also showed deep distrust of another tax to fund the mismanaged MTA, which just received a $15 billion bailout during the COVID pandemic. Residents talked about living in transit deserts and being fearful of using the subway, which has seen an uncontrolled increase in violent crime.

name: Josh Gottheimer
comment_text: The Federal Highway Administration has recognized that “the project could have effects on environmental justice populations.” The MTA likewise recognizes potential adverse effects on these communities. The Authority also clearly admits that this new tax will disproportionately harm lowincome drivers. We urge you please to demand that the MTA do its due diligence on this new tax on our hardworking families and provide a complete EIS. Thank you for your consideration. name: Assemblywoman Judy Griffin
comment_text: I write to you today as a State Assemblywoman and lifelong resident of Long Island’s South Shore, representing a district home to thousands of suburban commuters who travel regularly to New York City for work, school, family or entertainment. The economic and environmental health of both Nassau County and the City are irrevocably tied to one another, and major decisions about transportation and its funding should not be made as the result of just short-term decision making. Our region’s future is too important.

name: Assemblywoman Judy Griffin
comment_text: While our world has undoubtedly changed since the State Legislature first voted to proceed with a congestion pricing plan in 2019, ridership on the Long Island Rail Road (LIRR) has now returned to 75 percent of pre-COVID levels and new safety upgrades are being made to our transit – but automobile traffic seems worse than ever in the region. If congestion pricing is to proceed successfully however, the revenue collected from New York’s drivers must go into a “lockbox” for transit capital projects. The reliable, exclusive revenue stream that congestion pricing will provide to fund the MTA is absolutely vital – including that 1 in every 10 dollars will be devoted exclusively to bonding and investments for the LIRR. There are, however, outstanding concerns that I share with my constituents about the exemptions left undecided at the time of original passage that must be addressed and made clear before proceeding further:

name: Assemblywoman Judy Griffin
comment_text: ● Our first responders – police officers, firefighters, and EMTs – are often required by their shifts and emergency calls to drive directly into Manhattan at all hours. Their service must be respected and met with a clear toll exemption to ensure that congestion pricing is effective and fair. A user-friendly process must be established for residents with disabilities and handicaps to register for a toll exemption, especially given that too much of MTA transit is still not yet ADA compliant. There are students with special education classifications that must travel by car to the City. These families should receive an exemption. Residents from Long Island who are battling cancer, 9/11-related illness, and other serious diseases should receive an exemption when traveling into Manhattan for treatment. While I continue to advocate for these exemptions, I am always happy to discuss them further at any time. name: Assemblywoman Judy Griffin
comment_text: We are a group of concerned elected officials in Rockland County. We write to you in opposition of the current plan to charge Rockland County residents with the new congestion pricing, and we are putting forth our request that Rockland County residents be exempt from paying this surcharge. Unlike our neighbors east of the Hudson who have nearly 45 train stations, we in Rockland County have only 5 stations, none of which have trains going directly into Manhattan. Until the transit access to the city is vastly improved, congestion pricing will amount to an unfair tax to subsidize a transit system that does not equitably serve our community. Our residents will be charged thousands of dollars per year for their drive into the city without having a convenient transit alternative. For the past decade, we were forced to subsidize mass transit for the rest of our region as we contributed millions of dollars annually -- far more than the MTA invests into our County.

name: Assemblywoman Judy Griffin
comment_text: The complete disregard of the residents who live West of the Hudson has been evident in every step of the congestion pricing plan as we don’t even have a voice at the table when decisions are made on these matters. Therefore, we urge you to exempt Rockland County residents from congestion pricing as long as there is no viable one seat ride option into Manhattan. Thank you for your consideration of this matter. name: Assemblywoman Judy Griffin
comment_text: With respect to the CBD toll being a new tax, unlike a new tax, the proposed CBD toll would not apply to everyone. Rather, it would apply to people who drive into or out of the Manhattan CBD. Transit riders already have a cost associated with their travel to the Manhattan CBD since they must pay a fare to use the service, but these costs are not currently paid by drivers using certain routes. A toll to enter the Manhattan CBD for drivers is like the user fee (fare) paid by transit riders. Consistent with the Traffic Mobility Act, MTA would use the net revenue generated by the CBD Tolling Program to fund transit and commuter rail projects in the MTA 2020–2024 Capital Program and successor programs. Ten percent of the net revenues would be allocated to investments in Metro-North Railroad, which provides service in Rockland County. The CBDTP would improve travel conditions in Manhattan for all travelers to the Manhattan CBD by reducing peak-hour traffic entering and leaving the City. All vehicle operators in Manhattan would benefit from reduced travel times and reduced fuel consumption, which importantly includes Rockland drivers who visit and work in New York. Revenues invested in maintaining and enhancing NYCT buses and subways would also benefit those from Rockland County traveling throughout the City via public transit. See also responses to Frequently Received Comment 4, Frequently Received Comment 18, and Frequently Received Comment 23.

comment_text: ST September 9, 2022 Honorable Kathy Hochul Governor State of New York 633 3rd Ave 38th floor New York, NY 10017 Dear Governor Hochul:

name: Kamillah Hanks
comment_text: We are writing to ask that you withdraw your support for the Metropolitan Transportation Authority’s (MTA) “Central Business District Tolling Program.”

name: Kamillah Hanks
comment_text: The Environmental Assessment (EA) released by the MTA on August 10th makes it clear that the only objectives of the Central Business District Tolling Program (CBD) are to 1) reduce the miles vehicles travel within Central Manhattan by five percent; 2) reduce the number of cars coming into Central Manhattan by 10 percent; and 3) create a significant new funding source for the MTA. To create this marginal traffic benefit to Manhattan residents living within the proposed central business district, the CBD tolling program would charge an exorbitant toll for driving, which would effectively redisperse traffic congestion across other parts of New York City and the tri-state area, rather than reducing overall traffic. This toll, along with the negative environmental and financial impacts of this increased traffic in their communities, would disproportionately harm low and middle-income outer borough residents. Furthermore, at no point does the EA provide any conclusive evidence that this program would provide a source of revenue that is a stable and sustainable, nor does the MTA commit to specifically improving public transportation in areas of the city where it is significantly lacking.

name: Kamillah Hanks
comment_text: Once again, we should look to London, where the clogged main and arterial roadways across the city have had a particularly deleterious impact on communities outside the congestion pricing zone. Spillover traffic and motorists trying to avoid congestion now take circuitous routes through residential areas across the city and in neighborhoods in Outer London – what locals pejoratively call “rat running.” Rat running has led to traffic in otherwise quiet, arterial roads to double in the decade between 2009 and 2019, according to DfT data. The problem has gotten so bad that many borough officials began taking matters into their own hands, embarking on a new car-reduction plan called Low Traffic Neighborhoods by erecting barriers to prevent outside motorists from using their streets. The EA supports this:

name: Kamillah Hanks
comment_text: • Those travelling outside the CBD will see no reduction, and likely higher traffic volumes, despite the overwhelming number of New Yorkers who face congestion in Brooklyn, Queens, Staten Island, the Bronx, Nassau, on Long Island, the Hudson Valley, New Jersey, and Connecticut. In fact, even the optimistic data within the EA, shows traffic overall getting worse for Long Island, New Jersey, and Connecticut. In sum, the people who will pay the price get worse traffic. (Table ES-4) Mid-day and PM traffic volumes approaching the westbound George Washington Bridge will result in additional traffic throughout its northern Manhattan and South Bronx approaches. (4B-21) The EA estimates this will double pedestrian volume at already overcrowded NYC Subway stations in and around the central business district. (Table ES-4) The CBD Tolling Program Could Have Disastrous Health Impacts

name: Kamillah Hanks
comment_text: Even so, these estimates are troubling, especially when you look at the effect London’s congestion pricing has had on air pollution in Outer London and its suburbs over the last two decades. The toxic air pollution being caused by the increased traffic there is leading to nearly 4,000 premature deaths a year and children being born at lower birthweight, stunted lungs, and higher incidences of asthma, according to a recent study by the Imperial College of London. The CBD Tolling Program is a Regressive Tax

name: Kamillah Hanks
comment_text: Other concerning EA findings: • In every scenario, Staten Island will see more congestion from personal vehicles and trucks on highways and local streets. (Table 4A-25 & 4A-26) • In every alternative, the Bronx will see more traffic from thousands of additional commercial trucks, and in almost every scenario, the Bronx will see more traffic from personal vehicles. (Table 4A-28 &4A-29) Most of this additional traffic will be on the Cross Bronx Expressway, which has the distinction of having some of the worst asthma health outcomes in the nation. This tolling program will have little impact on the day-to-day life of wealthy commuters or residents within the Manhattan CBD. But the vast majority of the 1,856,000 people who enter the CBD by car each day – working- and middle-class residents of the outer boroughs and suburbs - and will now be forced to pay for these fortunate few. That is far greater than the entire population and beneficiaries living within the CBD. (EA Page 1-13). Even the EA begrudgingly admits, this toll would disproportionately impact on low-income New Yorkers, making this program a new regressive tax. (Table ES-4). Other EA findings:

name: Kamillah Hanks
comment_text: • The amount of total vehicle miles traveled throughout the 28-county study area will be reduced by between 0.2% and 0.4% by implementing any of the tolling scenarios as compared to taking no action, and by 2045, that number will only climb to a maximum of 0.5% at best. Meaning, it is a $1 billion annual tax on the region, without any regional benefit. (Table 4A-6, 4A-7 & 4A-14) The increase in daily commuting costs for auto drivers from New York City outside of the CBD will range from 7.9% to 37.2%, most significantly impacting lower income and minority drivers. Increases to Long Island, Hudson Valley, New Jersey, and Connecticut drivers will range from 5.8% to 26.5% (Table 4A-18) Drivers from New York City outside of the CBD can possibly face total daily tolls of up to $38.20, with the tolls having a disproportionate effect on lowincome families (Table 4A-19) No alternatives to generate $1 billion in revenue other than car-related fees were considered by the MTA that could spread the cost out more equitable and progressively through the regional population. The EA estimates the CBD Tolling Program would increase dangerous atmospheric pollutants – particulate matter, nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide, and volatile organic compounds – for Staten Island and the Bronx (Table 10-8). Considering the predicted increases in spillover traffic, particularly the hundreds of new trucks expected to fill the roads in these boroughs each hour, these estimates are laughably low and defy common sense (Table ES-4). Congestion Pricing Is Not a Budget Unicorn

name: Kamillah Hanks
comment_text: Congestion charge payments in London accounted for £232m (about $275 million) in revenue in 2021, or less than four percent of the total revenue for Transport for London (TfL), the city’s public transportation agency. Those figures came in after Mayor Sadiq Kahn increased the daily rate from £11.50 to £15 ($13 to $17.75) and adjusted the operating hours to includes 6PM-10PM and weekends to try to boost the agency’s income. The city’s congestion charge has failed to generate enough revenue to help TfL survive a precipitous drop in ridership and an economic downturn. The agency recently needed a $6 billion bailout from the federal government just to stay afloat. Considering London’s significantly higher traffic volumes, there is no chance the CBD Tolling Program would come close to generating the $1 billion MTA is projecting in the EA – especially when that figure does not incorporate exemptions that are being considered for New Jersey drivers, for-hire vehicles, and others. Given the MTA’s long, notorious history of fiscal mismanagement, cost-overruns, and failures to meet even the most generous project deadlines, it is simply magical

name: Kamillah Hanks
comment_text: Given all of these factors, to say that the Central Business District Tolling Program is problematic is an understatement: It is a disaster waiting to happen. We cannot in good conscience support a project that would be so harmful to so many New York City residents, and as leader of this state, we urge you to reconsider. Thank you for your time, courtesy, and consideration. Very truly yours, Joseph C. name: George Hoehmann
comment_text: On behalf of the Towns of Rockland County, we write to express our strong opposition to our residents being captured under the mandated pricing and tolling mechanisms to enter New York City. We respectfully request to be exempt from any additional pricing under the MTA Reform and Traffic Mobility Act or to be explicitly in any credits or discounts for tolls paid on same day tolls for bridges and tunnels. In addition, we also wish to express our disappointment that there are no members of the Transportation Mobility Review Board who represent communities that live west of the Hudson River. We request that a member representing these communities be placed on the Transportation Mobility Review Board so our residents have a place at the table as the policy is being created.

name: George Hoehmann
comment_text: In addition, we have seen the MTA continuously invest capital dollars, at the behest of our taxpaying residents, to help improve every transit option other than those that would meaningfully benefit our residents who are travelling to New York City for economy boosting means such as employment or general tourism. For example, the Penn Station Access Project provides easier transit alternatives into Penn Station for Metro-North’s East-of-Hudson commuters. Nothing of comparison has been done to improve Rockland County resident’s options for transit or to gain a return on the investment that they have shelled out for numerous years. That is why we also feel it is important that communities that live west of the Hudson River are represented on the Transportation Mobility Review Board. For all of these aforementioned reasons, we are requesting to be exempted from the congestion pricing measures enacted by the MTA Reform and Traffic Mobility Act and that the MTA ensure that a West of the Hudson River representative be appointed to the Transportation Mobility Review Board. Sincerely, As it currently stands, the residents of Rockland County have no plausible means of obtaining public transit to enter New York City and are already tax-paying members of the Metropolitan Transit Authority’s Community Transportation District (MCTD). Due to our location on the western side of the Hudson River, Rockland County residents must utilize a car to enter Manhattan because there is no one-seat rail ride to the Central Business District in addition to the already limited options that are operated by New Jersey Transit with their contract with MetroNorth. Rockland County residents have already been investing into the MTA with no return to show for it. For years they have been paying tolls incurred at the Mario Cuomo Bridge, George Washington Bridge and the Lincoln Tunnel. Other counties other than Rockland that are a part of the MTCD have undoubtedly better transit options as well as the privilege of utilizing toll-free bridges or transit routes that do not require any toll at all.

name: Robert Holden
comment_text: I urge you to halt the Central Business District Tolling Program, better known as congestion pricing. According to your own Environmental Assessment, this tax scheme will hurt lower and middle class New Yorkers the hardest. At a time when we are trying to do everything possible to make New York City a livable place for families, this policy literally says the door will hit you on the way out.

name: Robert Holden
comment_text: There is no economic, sociological or environmental reason for imposing congestion pricing. The sole motive is an ideological obsession with reducing the number of cars in Manhattan, people be While the wealthy, and a small professional class of soon-to-be wealthy urbanites, might have more room for street side brunches at their favorite Sunday-fun day spot, the outer-borough working class New Yorkers will pay the bill in the form of higher prices for food, goods and services. According to the MTA’s own study, traffic in New York City is not even reduced, it’s simply relocated to the outer boroughs, including sections of the Bronx which currently have unusually high rates of asthma and the highest poverty rates in the country.

name: Robert Holden
comment_text: New York is the leading state in the union for population decline. We have ads, on our own subways, telling police officers they should leave their jobs for easier gigs, which pay more, in states where the cost of living is less. New York is now routinely featured in national news for horrific attacks on the subway by deranged individuals. Your plan only exacerbates all of these problems. It adds to the true narrative that the governing powers do not care about everyday New Yorkers. Cars are necessary to commute from neighborhoods where public transportation is lacking and for families who have children. Imposing dramatically higher costs on commuters and families will result in an even greater share of this population leaving the city.

name: Robert Holden

name: Robert Holden
comment_text: We are writing to ask that you withdraw your support for the Metropolitan Transportation Authority’s (MTA) “Central Business District Tolling Program.”

name: Robert Holden
comment_text: The Environmental Assessment (EA) released by the MTA on August 10th makes it clear that the only objectives of the Central Business District Tolling Program (CBD) are to 1) reduce the miles vehicles travel within Central Manhattan by five percent; 2) reduce the number of cars coming into Central Manhattan by 10 percent; and 3) create a significant new funding source for the MTA. To create this marginal traffic benefit to Manhattan residents living within the proposed central business district, the CBD tolling program would charge an exorbitant toll for driving, which would effectively redisperse traffic congestion across other parts of New York City and the tri-state area, rather than reducing overall traffic. This toll, along with the negative environmental and financial impacts of this increased traffic in their communities, would disproportionately harm low and middle-income outer borough residents. Furthermore, at no point does the EA provide any conclusive evidence that this program would provide a source of revenue that is a stable and sustainable, nor does the MTA commit to specifically improving public transportation in areas of the city where it is significantly lacking.

name: Robert Holden
comment_text: Once again, we should look to London, where the clogged main and arterial roadways across the city have had a particularly deleterious impact on communities outside the congestion pricing zone. Spillover traffic and motorists trying to avoid congestion now take circuitous routes through residential areas across the city and in neighborhoods in Outer London – what locals pejoratively call “rat running.” Rat running has led to traffic in otherwise quiet, arterial roads to double in the decade between 2009 and 2019, according to DfT data. The problem has gotten so bad that many borough officials began taking matters into their own hands, embarking on a new car-reduction plan called Low Traffic Neighborhoods by erecting barriers to prevent outside motorists from using their streets. The EA supports this:

Those figures came in after Mayor Sadiq Kahn increased the daily rate from £11.50 to £15 ($13 to $17.75) and adjusted the operating hours to includes 6PM-10PM and weekends to try to boost the agency’s income. name: Sen. Brad Hoylman
comment_text: Thank you for this opportunity to submit testimony before the MTA, the New York State Department of Transportation (NYSDOT) and New York City Department of Transportation (NYCDOT) regarding the proposed Central Business District (CBD) Tolling Program. We are longtime champions of congestion pricing and believe that a successful tolling program will be beneficial for our districts, the city, and the entire region. At the same time, we will continue to advocate to make certain that equity and community input are central to the implementation of this approach to our city streets. We are grateful for the extensive outreach and community input that the MTA and partners are currently undertaking to best serve New Yorkers and ensure the success of the program. Congestion pricing is a smart approach to reducing traffic congestion and pollution while repairing and upgrading our mass transit system to provide greater accessibility and improved bus service. Scientists have been sounding the environmental alarm for years, and unless we take urgent steps to drastically reduce gas emissions, the effects of climate change will soon be irreversible.

If we are not successful here and our transit system slips further into disrepair, we could lose our competitive advantage as a city as well as one of the defining features that sets New York City apart from other big cities. It is crucial that all credits, caps, and exemptions are thoughtfully considered to ensure they do not undermine our ability to fund and modernize our transit system. We need congestion pricing to improve street safety. As we all know, over the past few years New York City has seen an increase in vehicular crashes and deaths. In 2021, seven years after the launch of Vision Zero, 273 people died in traffic-related incidents in the City. Unfortunately, according to the most recent data, the City is expected to outpace those numbers in 2022. By reducing traffic congestion and the number of vehicles on the road, there will be fewer car crashes, making the City’s streets safer for pedestrians, cyclists, and motorists alike. Finally, traffic is responsible for tremendous economic costs that will be curtailed through congestion pricing. On average, New Yorkers lose 102 hours each year due to traffic congestion, and congestion pricing can save up to $20 billion annually in congestion-related costs to our regional economy. This economic impact is more important than ever as our local economy struggles to recover from the mass unemployment and business interruption caused by COVID-19. For all these reasons, it is imperative that we come together to make the CBD tolling program a success, by addressing the concerns of New Yorkers across the city. name: Chantel Jackson
comment_text: The Central Business District Tolling Program (CBDTP), better known as congestion pricing, will benefit the greater New York City metropolitan area. While the overall impact of the CBDTP will be positive and will ultimately cause an overall reduction of mobile air toxins across the region, the proposed program increases air pollution within the Bronx. Even as the Bronx has taken steps forward with reducing carbon emissions, this is a step back for the neighborhoods surrounding the Cross Bronx Expressway, due to the increased air pollution from vehicles on the highway. The MTA's report notes an overall decline in air pollution across the city and region, but an increase for the Bronx. This is primarily due to increased vehicle miles traveled on the Cross Bronx Expressway, and the reality is there would be an additional increase on other highways, including the Bruckner Expressway and Major Deegan, through secondary transportation pressure, even if the methodology doesn’t show an increase. The CBDTP is therefore an issue affecting health, equity, and environmental justice issues for the communities we represent, which have historically taken on more than their fair share for decades. In order to have our support for the CBDTP, these Bronx neighborhoods need to see direct benefits that will result in a reduction of mobile air toxins. The best solution would be prioritizing the capital funding for the capping of the Cross Bronx Expressway. Money was allocated as part of the bipartisan infrastructure bill that Senator Chuck Schumer and Congressman Ritchie Torres were both instrumental in getting passed, but the project will need additional resources and it should be prioritized by the city and state. It is also important that the deck on top of the Cross Bronx provide additional long-term benefits, such as providing green space or by creating a public transportation light rail line. This line could provide an east-west railway link stretching from Washington Heights to Parkchester, creating connections across eight subway lines and serving the nearly 600,000 people that live in adjacent neighborhoods. In addition to fully funding the Cross Bronx decking, further priority should be given to projects that would reduce greenhouse gas emissions, such as providing free buses across the entire city, or, at a minimum, within Bronx environmental justice areas harmed by the CBDTP to further incentivize public transportation options for residents that need it the most. The city should also pass electric vehicle supportive legislation that will remove hurdles for where electric vehicle charging stations can be located and provide opportunities for electric vehicle investment across the city. This will encourage the transition to electric vehicles, which will be key to reducing emissions within the city. Other ways the city can support these environmental justice areas include prioritizing and further incentivizing renewable energy bonuses for building upgrades. The Bronx has many buildings with low-income residents and the city needs to support improvements to these buildings in order for building upgrades to happen. For NYCHA buildings, the city needs to prioritize and fully fund renewable energy upgrades. OFFICE OF THE BRONX BOROUGH PRESIDENT - 851 GRAND CONCOURSE, SUITE 301, BRONX, NY 10451 - (718) 590-3500

comment_text: What is most telling is that, in attempting to ascertain the impact of the CBD on New York City and the region, not once do authors of the EA cite the lessons learned from London, a city that has employed a nearly identical congestion pricing program for 20 years. That is likely because doing so would not support their Much like their counterparts in London, those pushing the CBD tolling program as a traffic cure all are seriously (and maybe purposely) overestimating the effects of economic incentives on people’s driving habits. This program rests on the assumption that a significant number of people really are making a conscious choice about driving, rather than doing so out of necessity or expediency. Yet evidence from London’s congestion pricing experiment suggests that the population that will get out of their cars and use other modes of transportation because of an extra charge to drive is very small. According to data from London’s Department for Transport (DfT) data, there are 5 million more vehicles on London roads then when the congestion pricing was first implemented 20 years ago. That’s a near 20 percent increase in people choosing to drive. That is a sea change in transportation behavior, just not the one that purveyors of London’s congestion pricing program were selling. Studies of the 25 largest cities in the world have found that what gets people out of their cars is proximity to viable public transportation. There is an inverse correlation between the number of people who live within a short distance of a bus or train stop and the amount of traffic and congestion, regardless of the cost of driving. In other words, congestion pricing benefits the few, fortunate residents who have the privilege of choosing between driving or a short walk to a train station, while most others are simply stuck paying the high toll of driving. name: Senator Anna Kaplan
comment_text: Good evening. I'm Senator Kaplan. I want to thank you for this opportunity. When we set out to enact congestion pricing in 2019, we were trying to address chronic problems impacting our region; traffic and the lack of investment in our public transit. Unfortunately the pandemic has only made these problems worse, straining finances at the MTA, putting new investments in the Long Island Rail Road at risk. So it's important that we do this right so that our region can benefit from new investment with the lowest cost to Long Islanders. The promised ten percent proceeds for the Long Island Rail Road, estimated at one hundred million per year, will allow for transformative investment to take place in our local infrastructure like the purchase of desperately needed new train cars. And overall, improvements to service and reliability for Long Island commuters. Importantly, it allows this investment to take place without hiking rates on Long Island commuters who take the train into the city. This money must be protected for Long Island and must be used exclusively for the benefit of Long Island Rail Road riders. And I will not accept any program that does not fulfill this promise. Additionally, in setting toll prices and exemptions, there must be regional fairness if this program is going to succeed. There can only be -- there can be no reference (sic) given to New York City or New Jersey residents that aren't also given to the suburban Long Island residents. Carving out certain people from responsibility while shifting the burden to others is unfair. And I will not support a program that mistreats Long Island residents and commuters. Ultimately, the tolling plan that should be enacted is the one that has the lowest out-of-pocket costs for residents who choose to drive into the city, while still hitting the targets needed for investments in Long Island's infrastructure. This program stands to be a huge win for our region, one billion dollars invested annually in our mass transit and our subways. But it must be reasonable for residents who are still struggling themselves due to the higher cost of everyday items.

name: Teresa M. Kenny
comment_text: September 1, 2022 Chairman Janno Lieber Metropolitan Transportation Authority 2 Broadway New York, NY 10004 CBD Tolling Program 2 Broadway – 23rd Floor New York, NY 10004 Dear Chairman Lieber and Members of the CBD Tolling Program:

name: Teresa M. Kenny
comment_text: On behalf of the Towns of Rockland County, we write to express our strong opposition to our residents being captured under the mandated pricing and tolling mechanisms to enter New York City. We respectfully request to be exempt from any additional pricing under the MTA Reform and Traffic Mobility Act or to be explicitly in any credits or discounts for tolls paid on same day tolls for bridges and tunnels. In addition, we also wish to express our disappointment that there are no members of the Transportation Mobility Review Board who represent communities that live west of the Hudson River. We request that a member representing these communities be placed on the Transportation Mobility Review Board so our residents have a place at the table as the policy is being created.

name: Teresa M. Kenny
comment_text: In addition, we have seen the MTA continuously invest capital dollars, at the behest of our taxpaying residents, to help improve every transit option other than those that would meaningfully benefit our residents who are travelling to New York City for economy boosting means such as employment or general tourism. For example, the Penn Station Access Project provides easier transit alternatives into Penn Station for Metro-North’s East-of-Hudson commuters. Nothing of comparison has been done to improve Rockland County resident’s options for transit or to gain a return on the investment that they have shelled out for numerous years. That is why we also feel it is important that communities that live west of the Hudson River are represented on the Transportation Mobility Review Board. For all of these aforementioned reasons, we are requesting to be exempted from the congestion pricing measures enacted by the MTA Reform and Traffic Mobility Act and that the MTA ensure that a West of the Hudson River representative be appointed to the Transportation Mobility Review Board. Sincerely, As it currently stands, the residents of Rockland County have no plausible means of obtaining public transit to enter New York City and are already tax-paying members of the Metropolitan Transit Authority’s Community Transportation District (MCTD). Due to our location on the western side of the Hudson River, Rockland County residents must utilize a car to enter Manhattan because there is no one-seat rail ride to the Central Business District in addition to the already limited options that are operated by New Jersey Transit with their contract with MetroNorth. Rockland County residents have already been investing into the MTA with no return to show for it. For years they have been paying tolls incurred at the Mario Cuomo Bridge, George Washington Bridge and the Lincoln Tunnel. Other counties other than Rockland that are a part of the MTCD have undoubtedly better transit options as well as the privilege of utilizing toll-free bridges or transit routes that do not require any toll at all.

name: Shekar Krishnan
organization: New York City Council Member - District 25
comment_text: Thank you for the opportunity to submit public comment on the Environmental Assessment completed on the congestion pricing plan for the Central Business District (“CBD”) of Manhattan. I represent the 25th Council District in New York City. The communities of Jackson Heights and Elmhurst are vibrant, predominantly working class, immigrant communities. Like many other districts in Queens, we are burdened by service delays stemming from the lack of public transportation infrastructure investments by MTA. Given this I am in support of the congestion pricing plan in Manhattan’s CBD to fund needed repairs and infrastructure improvements in our public transportation system and reduce our City’s reliance on personal vehicles for commuting. In this comment I want to focus on three points: 1) the importance of congestion pricing tolls in improving transit options for my majority non-car owning district; 2) the importance of reducing car usage in the CBD for advancing pedestrian safety; and 3) mitigation of potential adverse impacts on for-hire vehicles and taxi workers in the MTA’s final iteration of the congestion pricing plan.

name: Shekar Krishnan
organization: New York City Council Member - District 25
comment_text: The importance of congestion pricing tolls in order to improve transit options in Queens Congestion pricing is essential to meet the goals of the MTA’s Capital Plan. The single biggest piece of capital plan funding $15 billion is expected to come from congestion pricing. This investment will mean more reliable transit service on buses, subways and commuter rails. That $15 billion will help tremendously in alleviating transit delays and issues that are seen in my district. There are numerous subway lines that run through my district, with a major junction at the 74th Street - Roosevelt Ave station. Further, over half of my district does not own a car and relies on public transportation for commuting. Any maintenance delays along those lines can create commuting nightmares for my constituents and many other Queens residents who transfer at stations in my district. The funding from congestion pricing would ensure my constituents are better able to have efficient access into and out of the Manhattan CBD (where many commute on a regular basis). Further investments in the capital plan will improve bus service along corridors across the city and including in my district where there is a priority to improve service Shekar Krishnan, New York City Council Member - District 25, September 23, 2022 (Submission 14553) - Continued

name: Shekar Krishnan
organization: New York City Council Member - District 25

It is of the utmost importance for me that any adverse impacts on for-hire/taxi drivers are addressed in the final congestion pricing plan presented by the MTA.
