I believe the CBD should be defined to below Times Square to make it more family friendly.

name: Yaakov Ani
comment_text: Hi I am writing to point out a tremendous benefit to the environment if crossing credits are implemented. As you may know, every day tens of thousands of people drive out of their way to the Brooklyn Bridge as opposed to taking the the Hugh Carey Tunnel in order to save the toll. This causes large amounts of excess gasoline usage to reach the bridge plus large amounts of congestion around the bridge further guzzling gasoline and polluting the atmosphere. This is just one example as there are many more ways people go to free crossings or crossings that charge only one way to escape tolled crossings. I therefore strongly recommend that crossing credits are implemented in a way that people end up paying the exact same total amount regardless of which entry and exit crossings are taken. This would incentivize people to to take the shortest path which would use the least fuel and help the environment which is the point of the whole thing. Thank you for listening.

name: Bruno Annicq
comment_text: fully support congestion pricing. important source of capital for the MTA, encourages people to take public transit and the right way to price access to our busiest roads. will also help reduce road accidents.

name: Sasha Annor
comment_text: I do not support the CBD tolling program, I’m a resident of NJ and I have a young child who attends school in NJ however, I work in New York. I commute into NY via car, I pay three tolls each day and I pay for city parking which totals over $50 each day (excluding gas) that I receive no reimbursement or tax break for because I am not eligible. I don’t choose to commute via car, I have no choice. I don’t have any family living in NJ and my small down only offers child care till 6pm. So I need the flexibility of being able to respond to an emergency at a moments notice and the ability to leave work at a very specific time to pick up my child timely. Bus systems to and from NJ don’t offer that flexibility. And the train system isn’t an option in my town. I work in NY because the pay is competitive and allows me to afford my house and offer my child a quality education. The CBD tolling program would be an additional burden. If it goes into effect I will no longer engage in activities in NY outside of commuting to work because I simply won’t be able to afford it. And that includes even purchasing lunch for work. My budget is very tight as it is and I’ll be priced out of extras. This CBD Tolling Program isn’t going to encourage NJ commuters to take public transportation, those of us that drive do so out of a need, not a luxury. No one would choose to spend hundreds of dollars on the road if they had another option.

name: Christine Annunziata
comment_text: I think it is terrible to charge hard working people who are already paying exorbitant tolls to get to work. It's just another example of how our of touch the MTA and politicians are on how the middle class is struggling especially during this time of inflation. It is irresponsible to your constituents who elected you. The city should be offering incentives and tax breaks on commuters not penalizing them. In addition the congestion pricing will be passed onto the commuters in increased prices for services and goods. It is totally ridiculous to introduce this and penalize hard working Americans. I urge you to not pass this.

name: Tracey Annunziato
comment_text: Perfect. Thank you for allowing me to speak. I spoke last night, but I also wanted to speak again. My name is Tracey Annunziato. I live in Brooklyn, New York. I was just recently approved for permanent disability a year ago, as I have a very chronic, painful chronic pain condition that affects my leg, back, neck, shoulder, my entire body. I also possess this New York City handicap parking permit, which is very hard to get, and I just had to renew it. And went through a tedious process of having to send so many doctor's reports just to renew this handicap parking permit that I've had for years. I feel like this congestion pricing is really a hardship for people with disabilities and people like me and the elderly, that have and rely on their car. Parking permit is given to us because we have the severe disabilities and we require the use of our personal cars. This handicap parking permit is a hardship because I cannot ambulate to subway systems at all. Number one, not everybody gives you seats on the train. Number two, the steps are impossible. I cannot walk up steps alone, nevermind carrying the walker that I ambulate with up the steps with me. Number two, I see various doctors in Manhattan. I travel through the Hugh Carey Tunnel when I go to see these doctors. And now having to pay an additional money just to use my car, because I'm using my handicap parking permit in order to go see these doctors. I just think that if you have this New York City handicap parking permit, we should be exempt from paying this ridiculous extra toll. It's just tedious. Please just consider exempting the New York City handicap parking permit holders. Thank you for allowing me to speak. Have a good afternoon, everyone. Bye.

name: Tracy Annunziato
comment_text: Good evening. My name is Tracy Annunziato, and I am currently out on permanent disability and I currently possess a New York City handicap parking permit. I have extremely limited mobility due to all my back pain conditions. I can't tell you the amount of doctors that I have with NYU as well as -- in Manhattan. And every time now, I have to rely on my car to take to Manhattan I will have to pay. I would gladly take the subways. However, they don't have elevators, every station does not have escalators, and if you do have elevators and escalators, they are not always working. So I rely on my car in order for me to get around. And if I have to pay in addition to come through the tunnel, it's an extreme hardship for me. So I just think you need to consider that all of us that possess this New York City permit have it for a reason because we have -- we need it for our cars in order to get around in the city. I come from Brooklyn, we need our cars. Without our cars, we have no way of getting around. So thank you for listening to me and have a good night.

name: ANON
comment_text: Dear MTA, This program will only further hurt low and middle-income new yorkers. The wealthy people are going to keep driving into the city no matter what it costs. The poor people will be prevented. Not to mention the number of people that will loose their jobs because their employers cannot afford the new tolls. Please do not adopt this.

name: Anonymous
comment_text: This is a very bad idea not even thinking about peoples income. Their jobs does not give them a raise how do we expect people paying for this? How are they getting to work? Especially the train schedule from Suffolk does not cover anyone who start work at 3pm in NYC? People like me struggling to survive cannot afford it. Please stop, we are putting people in deep poverty.

name: Anonymous
comment_text: Way to make life more expensive. I'd say I travel to Manhattan at least 1-2 times a month. This would just cost me another $400 - $500 a year. No thank you. Please keep your Go Green ideas geared to affordable solutions and not pass the bill to the average New Yorker.

name: Anonymous
comment_text: Don't toll cars. We need cars provide safe transportation throughout the city. I haven't been on MTA transportation in months because it is dangerous and unreliable.

name: anonymous
comment_text: if transit prices and/or train ride times aren’t being reduced i don’t see what the point in this program is

name: Faraz Ansari
comment_text: I think the tolling program and congestion pricing in general is an excellent idea! However, it is counterproductive to treat motorcyclists and scooters the same as cars. For one, they release vastly fewer pollutants into the air than cars and trucks. They also take up about 1/3rd the amount of space for parking and traffic. Last, scooter riders are overwhelmingly delivery and service workers, who would be disproportionately financially affected as flat fees are generally regressive. By not exempting 2-wheel vehicles, the MTA and NY DOT are dis-incentivizing citizens from making the sustainable choice, while the richest people will still use their blacked out SUVs with impunity. Please provide an exception for motorcyclists and scooter drivers!

name: Douglas Antebi
comment_text: And here we go again with soliciting public opinion. Four years ago, you folks started holding feedback forums for people on the redesigning of the Queens Bus routes to accommodate residents of Eastern Queens. Four years later nothing has changed. And all the people involved in the Queens Bus Redesign project got paid tax dollars but there is still no redesign. So do I feel confident that my works herein are going to matter? Well, not really. But, at least, I tried to do my part to express my opinion. However, it will probably only find it's way in a pile of other papers or emails. Get stuff done Mayor Adams. You can do it. I know you wanna do it. But in my opinion, you are up against the reality of all words and no actions. I'm done here with my unpaid opinion and feedback.

comment_text: Getaround supports efforts in the City of New York to reduce traffic congestion, lower greenhouse gas emissions, and increase equitable and sustainable transportation options for residents, employees, and visitors. name: Jason Anthony
comment_text: Good evening, everyone. Jason Anthony from the Amazon labor union. A couple of things that we have to consider: One, you have Amazon employees that work in the fulfillment center in the west shore of Staten Island that commute by mass transit, either drive from all different parts of the city, even from New Jersey from the Goethals, Verrazano and from different parts of the city and even the Verrazano. If you're not a Staten Island resident, you have to pay almost $20 round trip. And interestingly enough, the Verrazano-Narrows Bridge is the most expensive toll by far in New York State. Have that in mind. And if we come from New Jersey, from all tollings, in other words from the GWB south, everybody will be affected. And keep in mind, the Hudson River Tunnel, if we have another catastrophe just like Sandy the whole northeast corridor will be affected. So keep that in mind while considering the tolling. In other words, consider something like dynamic tolling that they have in Central Florida. So they charge by the amount of traffic. So they don't charge overnight the amount of traffic that we deal with overnight. Especially, I live in Brooklyn, I see too much traffic on Flatbush Avenue and I see too much traffic too on 34th Street. And please have more of these hearings throughout the months of September and October. So I yield the rest of my time. Thank you very much.

comment_text: Those that pay a toll to get into NYC should have that amount or a portion of that be deducted from the cost of congestion pricing.

name: Lewis Anton
comment_text: While congestion is a major problem, I think there needs to be more thought into what the real gain is and who is going to be hurt the most with the increased pricing, and the method for doing so is to do in in-depth analysis of which autos are in the city to begin with. Delivery trucks have no choice. If the retailers and restaurants want to provide their services, they will need deliveries. Taxis may avoid the area, thus leaving those people looking for rides without, unless they have a waiver. I believe only a minor portion of the traffic is going to be held by people actually living in those areas. So other than money in the city's coffers, who is gaining and who is suffering from this pricing?

name: Chaz Antonelli
comment_text: I am more concerned with street parking then CBD. I would prefer to see street parking eliminated from Manhattan and other dense parts of NYC, in lieu of NYC government-owned parking garages, which charge a reasonable amount.

name: Philip Antoniades
comment_text: Congestion pricing is necessary to reduce pollution, keep the city safe and encourage public transit.

name: Joseph Anzalone
comment_text: I write in strong support of the CBD tolling program. The reduction in traffic will greatly improve the flow of vehicles that need to travel in the CBD, and the revenue raised will be a valuable source of funds for much-needed public transit projects.

name: Marjory Appel
comment_text: Dear CBDTP Team, Thank you for sharing the Environmental Assessment report on the congestion pricing program. While the environmental and fiscal impact of the program might be positive, I do hope that the adverse consequences for some NYC residents will be addressed. In the case of my family, our apartment is at 425 E.58th Street, and thus considered within the CBD. Congestion pricing would be particularly onerous for us, as my husband travels to Long Island 3-4 days a week to care for his elderly mother. If we were required to pay surge pricing merely to drive home it would severely limit our ability to provide regular care to my mother-in-law. I am certain that the CBD program was not designed to penalize this type of travel (especially to the far East side of Manhattan) --this would be an extremely harmful result of this program. If a decision is ultimately made to proceed with the CBD Tolling program, it would be of paramount importance to provide an exemption for people who live in the CBD. I look forward to learning more about how this critical issue will be addressed. Sincerely, Marjory Appel

name: Naftali Appel
comment_text: I am a Chesed of Williamsburg volunteer. I drive patients to a number of facilities that will soon fall under the new Congestion Pricing Zone. In order to remain a volunteer in good standings, I am required to drive a minimum of 500 miles per year, but on average, I actually drive over 2000 miles per year for the past 12 years. I pay all of the associated costs of my volunteer work myself. I use my own car, and the gas prices and tolls are costs I absorb on my own. These are not negligible expenses, but the cost is something I pay for to help those in need. Sadly, the new Congestion Pricing Plan will cost me far too much money, and I will be unable to continue driving for this worthy cause to facilities in the Congestion zone which I drive to now. Even if I were to scale down my trips, every single trip would cost ten times as much as such trips used to cost, meaning the end of the line for my Chesed work. The patients I drive are shattered by the fact that they will no longer be able to afford to visit the doctors they trust most. They have shared that they will no longer be able to keep up with their regular appointments. Their health will certainly suffer along with their pocketbooks. Family members of those hospitalized will no longer be able to afford visits to hospitalized family members, which will lead to patients being less willing to go to the hospital before it's too late to avoid the overwhelming loneliness they know will add to their suffering. We are letting down a population that needs us most by not creating a solution for those who look to us for assistance in regaining a foothold on life in the city they cherish. With hopes that something can be done before more suffer from the terribly high costs of the new Congestion Pricing Plan.

name: Alan Appelbaum
comment_text: Are those who reside within the CBD zones exempt from these tolls? If not the tolls will also discourage apartment sales in the area lowering home values. How do you plan to compensate the home/apartment owners for this action?

name: Diana Appelbaum
comment_text: We need congestion pricing, it’s the least we can do to save the planet. It’s also a better way to live. We were a 3-car suburban family. Moving to Manhattan enabled us to go car-free. Build more rail, and fund it!

name: Katherine Apple
comment_text: I'm writing in support of the proposed tolling program, because it will raise funds for mass transit. New York City has the worst traffic in the world and that's not a stat that we should be proud. I'm a biker and the crush of traffic makes it difficult to commute in Manhattan safely. I've seen the connections and commerce that happens when our neighborhoods have room for pedestrians to move and go to school safely and work and create in the open. Let's incentivize people to choose mass transit, invest in the MTA, and make room for humans all with one plan!

name: Eric Appleton
comment_text: I strongly support congestion pricing. Please don’t be swayed by arguments to the contrary. This is a good plan for all New Yorkers.

name: nicole aptekar
comment_text: Dear MTA, 3736-6018 I write as a resident of East Williamsburg, Brooklyn in support of the proposed Central Business District Tolling Program also known as congestion pricing. Congestion pricing will be good for our region. It will lower traffic, improve air quality, improve public transit, and set us on a better path to deal with the climate crisis. name: Lourdes Aquino
comment_text: Please allow me to introduce myself: My name is Lourdes Aquino. I am a compliant citizen, tax payer, mom, wife and full time employee. I love New York City. I am a 3rd generation New Yorker. I normally don't write about issues and go with the flow, but I feel I must send you all this message. I am writing, as I am extremely displeased with the choice the MTA & NYC is making in regards to congestion pricing below 60th Street. I lived in Lower Manhattan for 40 years of my life. I loved living there but had to move due to safety concerns and high rent prices. Therefore, in 2020, we moved to an apartment in East Elmhurst, Queens. We have lived here for 2 years now. My husband and I both work for the Federal Court, SDNY in Lower Manhattan. My daughter goes to school at Cornelia Connelly on East 4th street in Lower Manhattan, as well. This congestion pricing will affect my family financially and not in a positive way. Not only my family, but many families will be affected and forced to choose between paying high congestion prices over meals and other necessities. My husband and I have different work schedules, because we have to take care of our 10 year old. Neither of us have family or friends who help with childcare and we can't afford nannies or other activities. So, Monday through Friday, my husband takes the train to and from work - 6am train ride and 3:30pm train ride. ( So we do support the MTA ). And Monday through Friday, I drive into the city as I have to drop my daughter off to school/camp by 8am every day, while also making it to work by 8:30am. If I took my daughter to school on the train, I would not make it to work by 8:30am. I park my car in a garage at my job, so I don't use up any street parking. My car isn't for luxury, it is solely used for work and school transportation. I shared all of the above with you, because I am pleading with each of you, and the 6 people who are making this decision. I also feel like this congestion pricing is being placed on people because the MTA is trying to force people to have to use the train. For some, this may work, for people like me - it brings suffocation to my family and added stress. From a business perspective, I understand. But it still doesn't offer good customer service. I have been in public service for the past 20 years, and while there may be many reasons that congestion pricing is beneficial, please think about public service and what your constituents may have to face now that there is an added fee to an already stressed financial market for working middle class families.

name: Lourdes Aquino
comment_text: Good morning again, I forgot to add, if you choose to still move forward with congestion pricing, discounts go to lower income families, and just because I chose to work and have a job doesn't mean I don't get taxed like others and have rent and bills to pay monthly. I help contribute to society as well. I hope families like mine will be considered when deciding travel times for no pricing, or different pricing with the same fee as if we would take the train or bus. I thank you in advance for your considerations

name: Lourdes Aquino
comment_text: Good evening and thank you for allowing us to have the platform to share our thoughts regarding this congestion pricing. I'm sure everyone has had a long day, but we all know external customer service is just as important in internal customer service. So again, I thank you so much for staying on this late. You know, I'm a native New Yorker and I grew up getting around the city by train or bus. I have no problem with the MTA in that regard. However, I have a few concerns that I'd like to share. And after I have listened to other people's opinions, I can understand all sides, right, so there are three sides. Right. So we have the MTA's position on congestion pricing, those for congestion pricing, right, and then those who are not for congestion pricing. I'm somebody who makes lemonade out of lemons, so I go with the flow and I try to figure out how to work. Right. All New Yorkers figure that out, we face daily obstacles every single day. And I do agree with environmental benefits. I have a daughter and I want the best future for her, and all the other youth as well, they're the ones that are going to save the world. Right. But the $9 to the 23-dollar fee is really -- I normally don't do these kind of things, like speak in front of people, I have my colleagues I talk with. But for this level, I feel like, you know, what's going to be done is going to be done. Right. And it is good to speak up and that's how, you know, everybody can see each other's sides and how choices affect each other. I lived in Lower Manhattan for 40 years. I could understand the traffic issues, I hated it, around Grand Street, it was tremendous. Right. And then, I love bikes. But, you know, the bike lanes came. You know, I heard a couple of people make comments. Then it went two lanes to one lane, I caught myself, not having road rage but a little like -you know, they're cutting people off, there's no room. I get it, right, it's normal, we're human. But I moved in 2020, not because of the pandemic, but because where I live became extremely dangerous. I grew there in the '80s, in the '90s, I never thought I would leave, right, but I had to. And then, you know, Manhattan wasn't as affordable as normal, right, I wish I made more money. But, you know, next life, right, maybe I'll become a MTA panel board member like you. But every day, the point is I drive my daughter to school on East 4th Street. I take the BQE. I have to get there, to her school, by 8:15, then I have to be at my job by 8:30 in Lower Manhattan right by City Hall. You know, I'm sure somebody will say hey, get up earlier and take the train, whatever, you know, everybody has an opinion. But if I took the bus or train, which I tried before, from my daughter's school to my job, I don't make it there on time. And I don't want to be one of those employees that create problems. So all I really want to ask all of you, is that please take a -- I know people say no exemptions, but please take people into like me and working families like me into consideration. Charge us the same fee that you do for the train, to get on the train. My husband takes the train, that's what I want to let you know, every day he takes the train. So we're in support of it, but please -- and I know that some of you look tired, I can see all the -- Will, I see he's been looking different ways. You know, I'm on Zoom meetings too, I know when you lose -and there's been a lot of talk. But please, all of you, women, men, take into consideration hardship. Thank you so much and have a good evening.

name: Lourdes Aquino
comment_text: Thanks for allowing me to share with all of you again. I'm the third-generation New Yorker who, you know, spoke last week, who grew up in Manhattan for 40 years and understand the need for reduction of traffic. However, I'm also the mom that had to move because my neighborhood wasn't safe. It was worse now than it was in the 80s. I have to go into Manhattan every day to drop my kid off and go to work, you know. My husband takes the MTA, I worry for his safety daily, as I'm sure many of other New Yorkers do and have expressed. Also, while I drive in, I don't park in the street so residents can have a spot. I've lived there all my life, so I get it. After listening to everyone's comments and New Yorkers' opinions, some are pro congestion pricing, right, but many, many New Yorkers are against this plan. If it truly benefits the environment then, yes, let's unite and implement. But financially you're going to put many constituents and customers in such a financial hardship, that we may not be able to deal with. Many who are facing financial struggles that aren't -- none of us are aware of. Also everyone's talking about exemption for big businesses, low-income, taxi, residents, what about those people who come into Manhattan, like myself and other people; doctors -- on a doctor's appointment. You know, so I was thinking, you know, propose -- I propose that you create an exemption, right, where we provide proof of work, parking spots, doctor's notes or school letter, to qualify for something. You know to truly change the circumstances we're all in, we have to really valve money again because the value of money is lost. We must empathize and consider each other's situations and work with one another, not disregard a regular person who doesn't own a business or make under $60,000. This isn't a win for the quality of life for all people, if you truly think about it. And for those people who think that people who make over $60,000 have the money, no, you don't because you get taxed. Everybody needs to wake up and know that there are different tax brackets. What process excluded the regular worker or patient from these exemptions. It's going to cost my family $460 extra a month just to have this handled. So to fix financial problems, we don't continue to create financial problems. That's not where we're at. So, you know, I just want to leave everybody off with this. This is the last time I'm going to see you all. And there is a quote that my mentor in life shared and I'd like to share with every single one of you. You know, Dr. Daisaku Ikeda says, "Each form of life supports all others. Together they weave the grand web of life. Thus, there really is no happiness in one's self alone, no suffering that afflicts only others." So please rethink this plan, most of the people don't want this. Have a good night and thank you so much for staying on this call with all of us.

name: William Araaya
comment_text: Means of reducing congestion should be pursued that do not increase the onerous burden of fees, charges, and costs that has already been imposed on the members of the driving public. Moreover, the blame for the increase in congestion can be attributed not to the public, but to the actions and omissions of the NY municipal government due to the lane reductions and other roadway loss brought about by the construction of bike lanes, pedestrian plazas, and the like. Additionally, the DeBlasio administration allowed Uber and other so-called "rideshare" companies to flood the city with tens of thousands of additional vehicles -- most of them driven by amateurs not subject to the training or regulation to which our traditional driving industry has been. This vast number of additional vehicles has been a major driver of congestion, and it is the fault of the city government. On a personal note, as a night worker, the ability to drive to my place of employment has been essential, and because I travel at off-hours, I have not contributed to congestion during peak times. Also, with Staten Island (my borough of residence) being underserved in terms of hospitals, my elderly mother routinely visits doctors in Manhattan. My mother's ability to access quality healthcare will likely suffer as a result of an expansion of the cost burden as represented by congestion pricing. Since the dawn of the Bloomberg administration over two decades ago, and ramping up under the DeBlasio administration with its fraudently premised "Vision Zero", the driving public has been subjected to a long campaign of movement restriction and wealth extraction. The congestion pricing plan will take this campaign to new heights, collectively punishing the driving public, while offering no plan to focus compliance action on the bad drivers who use their vehicles recklessly or as platforms for noise abuse, etc.

name: Sam Aragon
comment_text: I think the congestion pricing plan is a fantastic idea and long past due. NYC has the best public transit in the US and yet many people still choose car travel because it's cheap. But it's only cheap because the social cost is not priced in. Adding a congestion fee is an economically efficient way to correct for the price we all pay for excess traffic - e.g., slower travel, noise, pollution, road repair costs, etc. I believe strongly in these fees and I hope they are enacted.

comment_text: My travel preference into Manhattan is by Metro north train. However, because of Covid 19 I have avoided train travel altogether and given up the businesses that I used that are located downtown. If I had to travel there now I would hire a car service to drive me.

name: Micah Arbisser
comment_text: If this program is going to work, exemptions need to be minimized. There should not be ANY exemptions or credits given to anyone who isn't required to get a credit or exemption under the Act. 5913-10950 CBD residents with incomes over $60k and no disabilities (including myself--I own a car, live in the CBD, make over $60k and am not disabled) should pay the toll like everyone else. The whole idea of the program is to discourage us from using our cars in the CBD except when necessary. 5913-10951 5913-10952 Police, firefighters, and other civil servants most definitely should not receive exemptions for their personal vehicles. These personal vehicles already illegally park on sidewalks and in crosswalks, bike lanes, and even parks in many parts of the CBD. It would be terrible policy to have a program that reduces congestion without requiring them to pay their fair share, further encouraging these vehicles to continue pouring daily into the most transit-rich area in the entire United States. 5913-10953 Those coming from New Jersey should not have their Hudson River crossing toll credited against the congestion charge. Again, the idea of this program is to discourage people from driving into the CBD. It would be crazy to have the program's costs disproportionately borne by those who actually live in the city compared to those who live in another state and don't contribute to the MTA tax base. 5913-10954 Please do not give out any more exemptions or credits than are absolutely necessary.

name: Rose Arce
comment_text: Hello, I'm a resident of which is in the zone under consideration for congestion pricing. I am writing to urge you to create an exemption for residents within the zone. 9225-6396 I have lived in this area for decades. The congestion problem is not related to residents; it is caused by people entering the zone for deliveries, car service, and tourism. That is clear from the studies and research that have been done, as well as apparent to anyone living here. Residents in this zone have cars because they need them - for transporting the elderly, children, the disabled, or because they have cause to leave the city occasionally. On any given day, most of the cars parked in our neighborhood have commercial plates, NJ plates, or get moved frequently as people come and go from uptown. In the case of my building, we would literally be charged every time we drive a block into the zone to get to our own homes. It's a tax on a specific group of people being singled out when they are not the ones causing the problem. There are many congested neighborhoods in this city and congestion pricing of some kind might alleviate the volume of traffic and improve the climate. But it is unfair and unproductive to saddle the people in the zone with the fiscal responsibility for addressing a problem they are not causing. I urge you to exempt anyone with a residential rental lease or ownership of residential property in the zone. Rose Arce cc'd is the president of the Horatio Arms Cooperative Board

comment_text: I am a doctor at a level 1 trauma center and take care of people injured by traffic violence every day. name: Luc Athayde-Rizzaro
comment_text: My name is Luc Athayde-Rizzaro and I am a resident of the Upper East Side of Manhattan. I work in Midtown and commute three days a week, and I also spend a good portion of my weekends traveling in and out of lower Manhattan. Me and my family, including my husband and my 70-year old mother-in-law, move around the city the same way the overwhelming majority of people do: by subway, by bus, by bike, and sometimes by cab. Not by a vehicle I privately own. The congestion pricing program is absolutely essential to ensure that our city is liveable in the long term, to ensure the air we breathe is actually clean, to fend off the existential threat of climate change, to protect residents from traffic deaths and injuries, and to build a more equitable city where people are prioritized over cars, and where public transit works for everyone. It is unconscionable that we continue to prioritize private car ownership over all other modes of transportation in NYC. Every year the city loses millions of dollars in revenue by providing free public parking for private car storage. Especially in lower Manhattan, the millions of pedestrians navigating public space are left with very little sidewalk space that they have to share with thrash, construction, and sometimes illegally parked cars or cyclists who are forced onto the sidewalk by dangerous conditions on the road. The congestion pricing program will bring much needed relief to this reality. In order for it to be truly effective, it should have as few exceptions as possible, so the program achieves its goal of improving public transit and disincentivizing drivers from bringing their private cars into the city. It should ensure that disabled people who have to drive in do not pay a toll, and it should limit in some way the tolls for cab drivers. But those are the only exceptions it should contemplate if we want the program to succeed. Let us ensure more equity in the use of public space in this city, fight climate change, and improve the lives of the overwhelming majority of people who move through Manhattan by public transit, foot, bike, and other forms of transportation that are not private vehicles. Thank you.

name: Thomas Bachant
comment_text: All right. Thanks, everyone. And great pronunciation of my last name, almost no one gets it right the first, so great job there. So I'm Tom, I a resident of the Lower East Side. I live near Houston Street. A street where people like myself, families, young kids, walk every day; and a street where one of my neighbors was recently murdered in a hit-and-run by a car. So I took a look at the Environmental Impact Report and it makes it clear that New York City has the option of going down two paths. One path is where we focus on livability for its residents, where you can walk around without pollution or risk of injury, people cab effectively take public transit, walk and bike to get around. Other option is becoming a city that's beholden to cars. Today 40,000 people die a year in car accidents. Cars are responsible for ten percent of all CO2 emissions, and car crashes are the number one killer of young children. If we embrace car dependency any further, the amount of space needed for everyone in New York City to own a car is bigger than the total square footage of New York City in general. This is not a sustainable option. I've heard some of the drawbacks, both of the impact report and from some of the people who have dialed in on these calls. A pretty clear one is people think it's too expensive for the car owners of this city. The truth is this is the ultimate opportunity for economic mobility for poor disadvantaged New Yorkers. Owning a car in New York City averages more than $10,000 a year to own and operate and drive through the city. If we focus on public transit, we reduce that cost to $1,000 a year, reduce that by 90 percent and allow these citizens to move freely throughout the city. We need to make it easier for people to migrate to those programs, which this congestion pricing toll will help to fund. Another comment I've seen is that it's potentially ableist against people who need wheelchair accessible vehicles. But again, the funds of this program can support our already wheelchair-accessible bus system, fund our underfunded paratransit and Access-A-Ride programs to make it easier for those folks to move around too. The people who are listed as impacted negatively by the impact report, which by the way, obviously far fewer people negatively impacted, but of those that do, those are folks who choose to take their polluting and dangerous car and drive it into a city of residents who don't want them there. They make this choice, they could take public transit, they choose to take their car. I don't see that as a serious disadvantage for those folks. So this impact report makes it clear that this is a major opportunity to increase the quality of life for our citizens, and I wholeheartedly support it. And thank you all for all the work that you are doing.

name: Edward Backlund
comment_text: As a civil engineer who has lived in Brooklyn since 2014, and who frequently commutes to Midtown Manhattan, I write in strong support of the CBD Tolling Program as proposed. For years, I rode the subway every day from Park Slope (later Bushwick, Fort Greene, and now Prospect Heights) to Herald Square for work. Even now as my work has relocated to Downtown Brooklyn, I still ride the subway frequently both intra-borough and into Manhattan and beyond. It is clear from a layperson rider's perspective that the subway system is painfully hitting the end of its useful life: when track repairs take months to achieve, when giant fires erupt out of nowhere, when retrofitting the system for accessibility seems equally as expensive as building an entirely new system in another metro area. Especially to a transportation aficionado, the need to overhaul the subway system is critical and urgent. Funding the subways with a massive infusion of bondable revenue, as proposed in the CBD Tolling Program, is our last chance to fix the system before it is too late. Moreover, as someone who drives frequently from Brooklyn through Manhattan (to the tunnels) en route to upstate destinations, I can attest that the proposed fee is in line with the time savings that I gain by driving through lower Manhattan (as opposed to having to take the GWB or VNB). I strongly support the proposed CBD Tolling Program as both a subway system user and tollpayer, and I look forward to its unimpeded rollout. May it serve as a case study for when a city "did the right thing."

name: Zoe Baldwin
comment_text: Hello. My name is Zoe Baldwin. I'm the New Jersey director for the Regional Plan Association. For decades, RP has supported congestion pricing because we see it as the centerpiece of the set of policies that will lead to a greener more equitable region. However, many in New Jersey have expressed valid concerns about how this will impact drivers in communities on this side of the Hudson. And as a life-long New Jersey resident, I fully understand those concerns and I'm here today to reiterate the congestion pricing benefits New Jersey a great deal. While New Jersey have always paid tolls to enter Manhattan, many from New York and Connecticut have avoided this by crossing at free city-owned bridges such as the Brooklyn Bridge. But with toll credits in place at all three New Jersey crossings, this new policy will truly level the playing field. Additionally, four out of five New Jerseyans already use transit to cross the Hudson River and congestion pricing will reduce traffic for that small percentage that do need to drive into the Central Business District. Congestion pricing will also improve the city's public transit system, which is used by the vast majority of New Jersey commuters once they cross the river, further facilitating a smooth trip for everyone traveling from our state regardless of whether they ride or drive. We do, however, strongly support the provision of toll credits for drivers at all three Hudson River crossings, including the George Washington Bridge, which will eliminate unwanted traffic shifts caused by drivers shopping for the cheapest tolls. The bottom line is that the ES shows that congestion pricing is a big win for the region. But again, we strongly urge MTA to choose a scenario that includes credits for all New Jersey crossings. Thank you.

I'm here to urge everyone of us to create a forward-looking city where all New Yorkers, not just drivers, are comfortable using the streets and where buses and bikes, as well as pedestrians can travel quickly and safely. name: William Ball
comment_text: This is very unfortunate for people like me who live right on 60th street. I frequently park on the street in the upper 60's and low 70's, but when I go out of town I need to drive the car to my home to load the luggage. So essentially my 2 minute trip onto 60th street to load my luggage, followed by driving back uptown and onto the FDR, will be taxed, despite my barely contributing to this congestion whatsoever. I understand you need to choose a cutoff, but between 61 and 60 does not make much sense. Vehicles coming from the Queensborough bridge for example, will be coming in below that cutoff. What makes much more sense is to have this cutoff between 60th and 59th, because 59th is really the beginning of the target region, not 60th street. 4763-8263 Additionally, I believe the $60,000 salary cutoff is too low for the tax credit. With inflation and current living expenses in NYC, even making an $80,000 salary is not easy to get by with. Considering sticky prices, New Yorkers are not expecting these costs to decrease dramatically even with reduced inflation. I suggest the cutoff be at least at the $80,000 salary at minimum.

name: James Ballantine
comment_text: Congestion pricing is badly needed to fund the MTA and to reduce congestion. Reducing congestion will speed up busses and reduce noise and air pollution. Additionally, the reduced travel times for those who pay the fee will be a huge benefit to those individuals whose time is valuable. You either pay with your time or with money, and at least paying with money can do some good for the subways, trains and busses which are heavily relied on by the poor. Those who don't make enough for the congestion fee to be worth it will benefit from faster busses thanks to the reduced congestion, and they will also benefit from the funding to the MTA. It is a win for essentially everyone even if they don't currently see it. Congestion pricing in cities like London or Stockholm has always gotten more popular once it is in place because people can see the effects of reduced congestion and pollution. I cannot stress enough how beneficial this will be for the city and the vast majority of people and desperately hope we implement it soon.

Simple and basic analysis does not mean that it is ineffective. It simply means that if the basic highway assignment validation volumes are not acceptable, when compared to the counted volumes, then the credence of the modeling will be lowered. The analysis is restricted to the bridge and tunnel crossings to/from Manhattan, to/from Staten Island, and to/from between Bronx and Queens Counties. These crossings are the most important links in the entire BPM network of Crossings. As such their acceptable or unacceptable validations will serve to judge the efficacy of the highway network validation. Other highway network crossings and internal screenlines and cutlines are of lesser importance. The final output of the travel model is basically the assigned volumes to the highway and transit networks. Generally, all major Measures of Effectiveness (MOEs) for plan or project evaluation are determined by these volumes. As such it is critical that the base-year validated model network assigned volumes when compared to counted volumes are reasonable and acceptable for the model period, by roadway direction, and per vehicle classification. Unacceptable base-year “validated” highway and transit volumes and resulting MOEs will inevitably lead to incorrect evaluation transportation project(s) and plans. The simple examinations of some of the BPM highway network validation results of the 6-10 AM period for some examples of travel to/from Manhattan, Staten Island, and the Bronx by their river crossings by vehicle class have shown that the BPM has not been validated to reasonable and acceptable degree of error ranges. Further such examination of BPM highway screenlines, individual or corridor highway segment volumes, etc have not been done as they are also expected to be very unacceptable from a disaggregate analysis. Travel demand modeling could be done with a range of models, based from simple sketch planning types to the newer complex activity-based models. Whatever types and number of mathematical models are used, the basic final outputs which the public and decision-makers really want to see and examine are the highway and transit assignment outputs, and their changes which result from plan or project(s) analysis. Generally, the numerous math equations and procedures are too complicated for the general public and decision-makers to understand, and they place their “trust” somewhat in the professionals to do un-biased and accurate work to produce the end results. NYMTC uses the BPM primarily for federally mandated air quality conformity analyses. Paul Balmacund, September 23, 2022 (Submission 15169) - Continued Year 2010 BPM Update EXHIBIT 24 DAILY TRUCK VALIDATION AT MAJOR CROSSINGS New York Best Practice Model 2012 Update Summary Report Final Report June 2021 6.3 Sensitivity Testing Sensitivity testing involves adjusting key factors in the model and observing the effects on forecasted travel. These adjustments can be made to model parameter values (e.g., mode choice cost coefficients) and to model inputs (e.g., land use variables, socioeconomic conditions, fuel costs, etc.). NYMTC defined the following sensitivity tests to be performed for the 2012 NYBPM: • Toll changes – Increase tolls on all (tolled) crossings. • Parking cost changes – Increase and decrease parking costs in the Manhattan CBD south of 60 Street. • Major development – This consisted of coding a hypothetical major development in Long Island City, including expected changes in population and employment outside the development itself. • AV “package” – While the effects of autonomous vehicles (AVs) on travel behavior are not truly known, there has been a fair amount of research that suggests assumptions about changes in the model to reflect an AV future. The following items were revised: o Roadway capacity increases, to reflect more efficient use of roadways by AV. o Revise in-vehicle time parameters for auto modes to reflect the utility of performing other activities in the car. o Change parking cost assumptions to reflect that AVs may not need to park at the destination. th 6.3.1 Toll change test Example In this test, the toll rates for all tolled crossings (bridges and tunnels) in the region were increased by 25 percent compared to the base year scenario. The objective was to see how key demand measures were affected by increasing tolls. There were slight decreases in volumes on major crossings with the increased tolls, on the order of about one percent. There was a decrease of about two percent on the crossings between New Jersey and Manhattan, where auto tolls cannot be avoided, and slightly larger increases for other crossings where auto tolls cannot be avoided. Changes in origin-destination patterns were very small. In general, the sensitivity of the model to toll changes on major crossings appeared to be reasonable. Traffic volumes decreased by a modest amount, reflecting that in many cases, tolls cannot be avoided on these crossings or would require substantial travel time increases to do so. The toll increases do result in a small mode shift from auto to transit. The BPM’s consultant team use of the 2012 Base-year BPM for the aforementioned sensitivity tests was a waste to time and resources to generate highly likely incorrect results and conclusions, on such a large scale that it cannot be taken seriously. The above Table is taken from the Year 2010 BPM Update for Daily Medium and Heavy Truck volumes validation for the East River and Hudson River Crossings. So, even the daily truck assignments had major differences for these crossings, much less the period differences. Sensitivity to toll increases depends on a wide variety of variables embedded in the BPM modelchain. Obviously, one of these Level of Service variables is both highway and transit travel-times. For example the highway skim-matrix provides travel-time, distance, costs, or a combination called Generalized Costs, for each O-D pair. Assigned volumes determine travel-paths and therefore traveltimes. Therefore, if assigned base year validated volumes are highly inaccurate on the highway network then O-D travel-paths and travel-times may be incorrect, thus leading to incorrect skims being input to the mode choice logsum equations. Therefore the 1% to 2% decreases in volume changes from a Toll Change test for NYC toll facilities would likely be highly inaccurate as the BPM’s +_ “validated” AM-period vehicle class volume differences and percentages were highly inaccurate, for the start, at the toll and non-toll facilities. So, the differences in assigned volumes at these facilities may due to the already embedded validation errors. Paul Balmacund, September 23, 2022 (Submission 15169) - Continued 6.3.3 Major development test CONCLUSION In this test, the modeled impacts of a simplified representation of a hypothetical major development with 15,000 employees in Long Island City were examined. A complete description of the assumptions regarding increases in service/retail employment supporting the additional workforce at the site, decreases in employment elsewhere in the region, and changes in population to supply the new workers are documented in the sensitivity test memo. The final output of the travel model is basically the assigned volumes to the highway and transit networks. Generally, all major MOEs for plan or project evaluation are determined by these volumes. As such it is critical that the base-year validated model network assigned volumes when compared to counted volumes are reasonable and acceptable for the model period, by roadway direction, and per vehicle classification. Unacceptable base-year “validated” highway and transit volumes will inevitably lead to incorrect transportation project(s) and plans MOEs evaluation. The objective was to examine the sensitivity of the model to location-specific changes in socioeconomic data inputs. Volumes on some of the major routes in the general area of the development site were examined; generally, the volumes in Brooklyn and Queens increased by about one percent under the major development scenario while major roadways in Nassau County increased by about half a percent. Volumes on the East River crossings near the site decreased by about three percent. Transit trips increased in Queens and Brooklyn while decreasing in the rest of New York City. In general, the model results appear to change in the correct direction under the major development scenario. Traffic volumes and transit ridership increase near the development site and decrease in places where employment is assumed to decline. There seems to be a slight mode shift from transit to auto, reflecting that some employment is shifted from Manhattan, where transit service is the greatest, to Long Island City, which has transit service but at a lower level than Manhattan. The magnitude of the transit decreases in Manhattan, however, seems to be too high, and VMT decreases may be too large. As part of the next model update, It is worth looking further into the sensitivity of the model regarding trips to Manhattan, especially work trips. Again, this sensitivity test was a waste of time and resources. What were the assumptions of decreases in employment “elsewhere” in the region and changes in population to supply the adjusted labor force, based on? The only way such sensitivity tests could be done reasonably is with a well calibrated/validated integrated land use–transport model system. Just whimsically increasing and decreasing employment, labor, and population in various zones/districts in the region makes no rational sense. NYMTC, in the early development of the original BPM had toyed with the idea of implementing an integration of Alex Anas’ METROSIM land use model to the BPM transport model. Unfortunately, that never occurred. The volumes increase and decreases experienced on the network, as found in the test, cannot be accepted with any credence. The (+_)errors in the BPM 2012 highway validation on the East River Crossings were far greater than the -3% experienced. So, the -3% decreases could be nothing but validation error related. The same reasoning could be said for the 1% volume increase on the roadways in Brooklyn and Queens, and 0.5% in Nassau County. Traffic volumes and transit ridership increase near the development site and decrease in places where employment is assumed to decline. A model is not needed to predict this outcome. The simple examinations of some of the BPM highway network validation results of the 6-10 AM period for some examples of travel to/from Manhattan, Staten Island, and the Bronx by their river crossings by vehicle class have shown that the BPM has not been validated to reasonable and acceptable degree of error ranges. Further such examination of BPM highway screenlines, individual or corridor highway segment volumes, etc have not been done as they are also expected to be very unacceptable from a disaggregate analysis. Large MPO consultants too often spend millions of dollars to develop massive travel demand modeling systems, with very extremely complex procedures, which take days/weeks to prepare basic inputs and days to run on very expensive computer “farms”. Sadly, the basic final outputs of these model systems are basically useless. This has been the case of the BPM versions since the BPM’s inception from around year 2002. What is the use and value of the Y2012 Update implementation of new ABM model routines and procedures, updated and new data collection, network improvements, etc, when the base-year period(s) final volume outputs are very poorly validated, to the point of being virtually useless ?. Too often consultants tend to hide behind the aggregate validation statistics, but the individual “building-blocks” to these aggregates tend to fail miserably when checked in detail. Obviously, there has to be some levels of acceptable error, but the errors which have been shown in this examination, above, are not tolerable at all. Overall, the BPM Consultant team gets an F grade for failing to produce reasonably accurate baseyear 2012 highway validation results for the specific modeled period, for directional highway facilities, by vehicle class. This shows that massive and complicated model systems which cost small fortunes and years to produce do not necessarily equate to producing reasonably accurate results which could be of use for decision-making. As the saying goes, “the proof is in the pudding”, and the BPM “pudding” does not make a passing grade, even from an initial, basic examination. The previous consultant team, in developing the initial BPM, had spent about 15 years and several millions of dollars in data collection, equipment, staffing resources, NYMTC staffing to monitor progress, etc, and had literally produced a useless BPM for AQ analysis, subarea, and corridor studies, etc. It was expected that the new consultant team would have corrected all the shortcomings of the past and produce reasonably accurate highway assignment results. However, now, it seems that NYMTC is in another consultant contract to spend more millions, over another period, to “update” an already useless and complicated modeling system to produce the same useless results. MPOs need to hire experienced, independent, and qualified technical managing advisors from the start of these model update projects to review work plans and monitor Consultant(s) progress and results throughout the process. Most of the time the technical advisory committees, from government Paul Balmacund, September 23, 2022 (Submission 15169) - Continued agencies, which are formed to monitor such work are not experienced enough to foresee the flaws and to ensure that stringent standards are to be followed by consultants.
